subtopic: DATES OF VISIT BY HER MAJESTY AND DUKE OF EDINBURGH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to announce to the House that Her Majesty the Queen and His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh have graciously agreed to visit Canada in 1970 for the purpose of joining in the centennial celebrations of the province of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. Her Majesty and the Duke of Edinburgh plan to spend ten days in Canada, arriving in Frobisher Bay on Baffin Island on the afternoon of July 5 and departing from Winnipeg on the evening of July 15.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
maintopic: COPPER AND NICKEL EXPORT CONTROL-STEPS TO ASSURE SUPPLY FOR CANADIAN USE
speechtext:
The strikes in the copper and nickel industry that have recently been settled have caused, as this House knows, disruption in the supply and trade patterns of these metals, not only in Canada, but in the world. During the period of the strikes the
government did not interfere with the usual trading patterns for these metals in view of the undesirable implications for industrial and trade relations.
The strikes are now over but the House will appreciate that it takes some time for the producers to reach normal production levels. The government wishes to ensure that as soon as reasonably possible, taking into account the dislocation to be overcome, the legitimate needs of Canadian users of these metals be met in full.
Accordingly, under the authority of the Export and Import Permits Act, Canadian copper and nickel producers will be required to supply all the legitimate needs of the Canadian consuming industry by January 1, 1970.

In the case of copper which is now under export control, this reflects the policy indicated in my statement to the House on April 1, 1969.
In order to ensure an adequate supply and distribution of nickel to the Canadian consuming industry and to prevent the drain of such supply to higher priced foreign markets, the government has amended the export control list to include nickel in all forms to all destinations.
As hon. members are aware, about 95 per cent of Canadian production of nickel is exported and it is important that our export customers be dealt with equitably in this period of readjustment. Therefore, in addition to the question of supply of metal to Canadian users, this action will have the effect of ensuring that the normal channels of trade are utilized fully to supply traditional export consumers of nickel and of avoiding diversion to higher priced markets outside Canada. Canadian nickel producers are working to reestablish the usual supply pattern to their export markets as soon as possible.

I do think, however, that it might well have been possible, despite what the minister said at the beginning of his statement, to indicate at some earlier stage what the intentions were so that there would be less of a problem in the normal flows of trade in these products.
I also point out that Canada as a trading nation must be very careful, particularly in the very unfortunate situation we are in now with some of our primary resources which are the subject of considerable trade export from Canada, that we not do anything to dislocate the normal flow and antagonize people in those countries with which we have such a strong flow of trade. I am sure the minister needs no caution; he has had enough from this side of the House in the last year or two. With that caveat I leave this issue.

maintopic: COPPER AND NICKEL EXPORT CONTROL-STEPS TO ASSURE SUPPLY FOR CANADIAN USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement today is a clear indication of the government's power to act when it chooses to take a stand. I for one am happy to see that the government is moving in this direction because for years we in Canada have been faced with a situation that as the major producer of nickel in the world we have been unable to supply the needs of our own Canadian secondary manufacturing industry. This action will go some way to meet that problem. The effect of this move will be to stimulate Canadian secondary


manufacturing industry. I hope the minister will liberally interpret its legitimate needs because the possibility now exists that Canadian secondary manufacturers will wish to enlarge their production, and their use of nickel. I hope the government will take this into account.
But, Mr. Speaker, the minister has to take a second step. For a long time we on this side advocated the first step he has taken. It has been a long time coming and we are now glad to see it happen. But the minister has to go beyond this and establish a two-price system for nickel in Canada, one price for exports related to world markets and another price for Canadian manufacturers based on the cost of production in Canada, because at present the cost of nickel does not depend on the cost of its production but responds to costs around the world. It is an intolerable situation for a country like our own that we have to be tied to the international speculative price of nickel. There should be a fair price for our manufacturers that will give them a chance to develop and enlarge their operations.
I hope that within a short period of time the minister will be able to stand up in the House and say we are moving away from the traditional government position of subsidizing and encouraging raw material exports to a position of encouraging secondary manufacturing in Canada.

I hastily took note of the minister's statement which makes us realize that we are now at a rather difficult stage of in the evolution of the labour movement. This should give cause for reflection to the true advocates of collective bargaining. The many conflicts which develop into strikes of all kinds are not indeed an indication of mutual understanding.
The government is compelled today to take a positive stand so as to avoid difficulties in business. Of course it has our support, under the circumstances, but I take this occasion to state that those in favour of strikes today will find reasons to go on strike tomorrow.
A perpetual renewal leads us to deadlocks and contributes to maintain, to the detriment of interested parties, a climate of collective misunderstanding, unwanted by the majority.
Exceptional conditions now prevail due to a strike we have heard about, but a clear stand should be taken and the labour legislation should be amended so as to meet the needs of our society.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed in 1934 by the then Conservative government to assist farmers who had suffered economic loss over a period of years. The government utilized federal jurisdiction to reduce debts to manageable proportions, reduce interest and arrange for orderly payment over an extended period of time.
The act remains on the statute books although it only applies to debts incurred prior to 1945. Because of severe financial hardship at the present time as the result of weather conditions, combined with the inability to market farm commodities-this situation is particularly applicable in northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan and in certain areas has persisted over several years-many efficient farmers have been unable to meet their obligations as they fall due. There is a significant increase in foreclo-

The bill further provides that the act will be brought into effect only in such areas as the Governor in Council may designate.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by expressing to all members of the House my appreciation for their co-operation in expediting the discussion of this bill today with a view to facilitating its passage through all stages as speedily as possible.
As hon. members will be aware, the cash advance program is a very important one in the prairie region of Canada. Under it, large amounts of money are available to individual farmers prior to sales opportunities, thus placing the cash for their grain products in their hands. The cash advance plan is being used to an increasing extent in the current situation. The farmers therefore have come to rely more and more upon this technique for obtaining cash, particularly in the earlier part of the year. It is, of course, well known and should be remembered by all members of the House that these are advance payments made to the farmer while the grain is still in his bin, still in store on his farm, and payments which he repays during the course of future deliveries of that crop in storage.
It is, of course, true that the general revenue is involved to the extent of bearing the cost of the interest on the money which is advanced in this way. The extent to which farmers have come to rely on these advances is indicated by the total figures on advances now outstanding. As of November 28, 1969, the last date on which I have a report, the total of cash advances in the hands of farmers stood at $231,446,136. The very fact of the extended reliance by farmers upon the cash advance system has led to a number of changes to meet the needs.

Would the minister allow a question? Is this the amount that has been advanced this year or does it include the amounts which have been advanced throughout the years?
December 5, 1969	COMMONS DEBATES	1643

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The figure which I gave was the amount totally outstanding on the date in question, that is to say on November 28, 1969. Of that amount some $28 million is outstanding from the previous crop year, and the difference, about $202 million is the balance still outstanding on this year's advances which total around $213 million, $11 million of which has already been repaid.
The importance of this scheme led last year to the doubling of the amounts of money available on a per bushel basis and the total amount available to farmers under the plan. This has accounted for the increased use of the cash advance plan. The importance of the plan to farmers has, of course, meant that those who cannot take advantage of it are accordingly in serious difficulty. In particular, the general cash advance plan requires that the grain upon which the cash is advanced, the grain which is used as security for the advance, be grain that is harvested and in store on the farm.
In certain areas of the Wheat Board region this year a significant number of acres of crop have not yet been harvested, and of course in some of those areas conditions make it quite unlikely that the crop will be harvested until spring. Weather, of course, is a fickle creature, and some harvesting has in fact been going on even these last few days. But none the less, in a broad enough area, a large acreage of land could not be harvested.
For the individual farmer this has meant a very significant problem in cash flow, added to a cash situation which in any case is serious. Accordingly Bill C-157 is brought forward with a view to providing provisional cash advances on the basis of grain which has not been harvested. This is therefore, an extension for this year of the cash advance principle to the security of unharvested grain.
The record of the farmers who have taken advantage of cash advances is one which leads one to have little concern at all about the fact that this unharvested grain gives theoretically some less security. The record, in general, of repayment of the cash advances is a superb one. We did have an example ten years ago of a provisional payment cash advance plan with unharvested grain as security, and under that plan only about $271 of the amount of money which was advanced was not repaid as the grain was harvested and the farmer was in a position to repay it.
At that time, under that previous plan, something just in excess of $1 million was
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop advanced. It is difficult of course to calculate with accuracy the extent to which individual farmers will take advantage of this provisional advance, but it does not in a real sense add to the expected expenditures by the government. Had these farmers been in a position to harvest their crops they would in general have been in a position to take cash advances under the regular plan. This bill will allow them to take those advances on unharvested crops.
The government will bear the interest on these advances while they are outstanding, and there is some small increase in expenditure involved here due to the fact that these farmers may not have crops to deliver to meet quotas during the course of the next five or six months, until in fact their grain is harvested and is available for delivery.
The cash advance envisaged by the provisional act follows very carefully the pattern set out in the main cash advance plan itself. The amounts per bushel, etc., are meant to follow the basic cash advance plan. Some special repayment provisions are provided to ensure that it is clear that a farmer need not deliver to meet his commitment with regard to the provisional advance until he has had an opportunity in the spring to harvest his crop.
The provisional advance maximum proposed in the bill is $3,000 with a total maximum between provisional advance and regular cash advance at $6,000, which is the regular figure for the cash advance plan itself. It is, I think, particularly appropriate to extend this provisional advance to farmers, as it was appropriate some weeks ago to indicate that Prairie Farm Assistance would be calculated on the basis of conditions known, with the grain unharvested, instead of waiting for the harvest.
In the case of these cash advances it was, I think, particularly important to let the farmers know that this provisional advance would be available, and to bring it forward into legislation. It was important to let them know it would be available because it would be undesirable to have their need for a cash advance lead them into the wrong farming techniques. It is better that they have the ability to take a cash advance on unharvested grain and make their own best farming judgment about whether or not the grain should be brought into the bin in the conditions which may exist at any given time as the
1644	COMMONS
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop autumn proceeds into winter. This provisional cash advance plan will do this, and it will provide to the farmers who are in this difficult situation some cash to tide them over until harvesting may hopefully begin again in the spring.
The records from the prairie region indicate that of the crops still in the fields, a large quantity is in wheat, oats and barley. The farmers have in fact concentrated on the oil seed crops for a number of reasons, including the marketing conditions which they expect for these crops in the near future.
I am therefore very pleased, indeed, Mr. Chairman, to put forward this bill for the consideration of the House, and again to express to hon. members my appreciation for their co-operation in expediting its enactment into law.

Mr. Chairman, in introducing Bill C-157, an act to authorize provisional payments for the 1969-70 crop in respect of unthreshed grain, the government is taking a hesitant step in the hope of staving off complete disaster this winter in those areas where the farmers unfortunately were unable to harvest their crops this fall.
We are pleased that action is finally being taken to provide some help to those farmers who, through the vagaries of the weather, have been placed in an intolerable financial situation. With winter upon us, it is to be hoped that the government will work with all possible speed to get the crops inspected and the cash advances made at the earliest possible date. It is for this reason the members of the opposition are co-operating in the hope that the bill will go through today.
As commendable as this action is, action for which members on the opposition side have been pressing since it became evident that large areas of crop would remain unthreshed, it does not even begin to deal with a problem of much greater magnitude. I refer specifically to the serious cash shortage all across the prairies because of the farmers' inability to market the grain they have harvested. Reliance on cash advances, as indicated in the minister's remarks, only emphasizes the serious cash position with which our farmers are now having to deal.
In spite of the fact that a real crisis has developed in western agriculture over the past two years, and is progressively becoming worse, there has been little indication that the

DEBATES	December 5, 1969
government is prepared to assume its responsibilities and come to grips with the problem. Neither is it offering any constructive leadership for an organized search for the solution.
One need only look over the recent Speech from the Throne to see that all the government has to offer is pious hopes to improve international co-operation and to re-establish orderly marketing. The only thing in it of any substance for agriculture is a vague reference to amendments to the Canada Grains Act which, and I quote:
-are intended to make our products more competitive in the world markets.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
That, Mr. Chairman, is the reference, in toto, to agriculture in the throne speech, one of the most important segments of the nation's economy. There is no mention of the economic toll inflation is having on an industry that has had little or nothing to do with causing it, and even less means to combat it. There is no mention of research into production and marketing for an industry plagued by surpluses, which the government tends to treat as the problems of a poor relative. Certainly, there is no reference at all to higher production costs, lower income, lack of cash and accumulating debts at the highest rates of interest in history. Surely, agriculture deserves better consideration from this government than just a passing reference to a document setting out its current legislative plans. Only now when the crisis in agriculture has developed into disaster proportions in some areas has the government finally decided to act-and even in those areas the amount of money advanced as a loan as a result of passage of this bill will be inadequate to assure the continuation of those farmers in business.
The Minister of Agriculture announced on November 7 that this legislation would be introduced. It was placed on the Order Paper on November 24, and is now being brought forward by the government almost a month after the minister's announcement. This is only another indication of the callous disregard of this government for the problems of the west and as far as assistance for agriculture goes, it is not only too little, it is almost too late.
Perhaps the reason for the government's lack of over-all agricultural policy stems from the fact that the cabinet, knowing little of agricultural problems, is afraid to take advice, no matter how well-meaning, that might lead it into making a difficult decision.
December 5, 1969

When the opposition members suggested a transport controller be appointed to straighten out the shipping mess during the crisis in Vancouver last winter, no one on the government benches listened. When it was suggested that the government assist the cash-short farmers to reduce wheat acreage in the spring, it fell on deaf ears. When we suggest that no business, farming or otherwise, can survive when it cannot sell enough to pay expenses, the government says it has set up a Grains Council. One wonders if the whole western economy has to hit the skids before this government acts.
Agriculture is looking for leadership, for action on the part of this government to help maintain it as a viable industry, and an important part of the Canadian economy. The value of the industry to the nation can best be illustrated by figures in a 1966 census. That year, the total capital value of Canadian farms was close to $20 billion. The value of all Canadian agricultural products approached $3.5 billion, and agriculture earned a dollar out of every $8 earned by Canadian trade. The Bank of Commerce, in a recent newsletter on Canadian agriculture, points out that Canadian farmers spent $2.7 billion on goods and services in 1968, and in the same year contributed $1.4 billion to our export trade.
These are facts that are surely of interest to all Canadians and points out the necessity of maintaining a strong agricultural economy, not only in the interests of the farmers, but in the interest of the nation as a whole. The report points out that this contribution to the economy was made by an industry that has had its labour force halved in the last 20 years to 7 per cent of the total employed in Canada, while at the same time has increased its production over 50 per cent. This advance in farm labour productivity is illustrated by the increase in the number of persons who can be supported by the production of one farm worker.
According to the Department of Agriculture figures, provided by the economics branch of that department, in pre-war years one farm worker could support the equivalent of 11 persons with food and fibre; today, the number is 42 persons. I offer these figures to show that farm efficiency alone cannot extricate agriculture from the economic strait jacket in which it is now. I offer them, too, to show that it is in the nation's self-interest for the government to quickly find solutions to our marketing problems in order that this efficiency can be maintained.

Until recently the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt have more or less been responsible for our grain business. Opposition suggestions that one minister, preferably the Minister of Agriculture, be given control always encountered complete government indifference. When I say more or less, I mean just that because I sincerely believe it was this arrangement that actually impeded any solution to our marketing problems. There is no doubt that this arrangement also worked against taking action at a crucial time in formulating a comprehensive grain policy.
I am supported in this belief by an article appearing in the Globe and Mail for November 14, 1969, which suggests the government is expected to announce a special grains secretariat to devise a grains policy. The article reads, in part:
Western farmers are facing another bleak year and a probable continuation of fairly critical cash shortage, along with jammed wheat storage and considerable uncertainty as to the outlook for the next crop year.
After a year of dealing with one wheat crisis, on a day-to-day basis, the government still has no basic policy to deal with the difficult position of western farmers or to phase some of them into other types of agricultural production or out of agriculture altogether.
Government insiders contend that intense wrangling between different government departments, each with some area of responsibility for grains policy, has prevented the formulation of any kind of longer term policy during the past year.
The article goes on to say that the departments even quarrel as to which minister's name should be on what announcement.
The farmers have been continually advised to switch production from wheat to other grains, and they have done a commendable job in wheat acreage reduction this past crop season. However, unless the government is basing its advice on a comprehensive market survey, one wonders whether we will eventually wind up with the same surplus situation in feed grains as we now have in wheat. Even now many farmers are still holding two-year-old oats and barley, or selling those products below Wheat Board prices to the feed mills.
Nor has Canada's export of feed grains shown too much promise in the past. According to Mr. J. E. McWilliam, President of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, Canada's exports of feed grains remained virtually static around one million metric tons per year from 1960 to 1966 inclusive. In the same period, United States exports had risen from 11.2

The Wheat Board, in its supplementary report for the crop year 1967-68, that is the last available report gives the following information with regard to the production and marketing of feed grains for that period. This information could indicate, particularly in the light of higher plantings to coarse grains in the past season, that stocks of these grains are already building up substantially. They show that the 1968 Canadian oats production of 362.5 million bushels was 58.3 million bushels above the previous year's crop. World oats production increased from 3.3 billion bushels in 1967 to 3.5 billion bushels in 1968. Canadian oats exports from August 1, 1968 to January 31, 1969 amounted to 1.3 million bushels as compared with 1.9 million bushels during the same period in the previous year.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
These figures indicate that while we increased our production of oats, we actually reduced our exports of that grain. The same applies to barley. According to the same report, Canadian barley production in 1968 amounted to a record 325.4 million bushels, of which 301 million bushels was grown in western Canada. This was 76.7 million bushels above the barley crop harvested in the previous year. The substantial carryover of 130.6 million bushels resulted in a record total barley supply of 456 million bushels, or 19.9 per cent greater than the total supply a year earlier. World production in 1968, estimated at 5.1 billion bushels, was 7.5 per cent greater than the 1967 crop. Canadian barley exports during the period between August 1, 1968 and January 31, 1969 totalled 10 million bushels, as compared with 18.6 million bushels in the comparable period one year earlier. Clearly, these figures indicate that although we increased our barley production, our barley exports were reduced. Anyone, therefore, who advises farmers to change to the production of certain grains should do so only after a great deal of work has been done to determine whether the advice is valid.
I have been given assurances recently by the Wheat Board that our exports in barley at least are improving and, hopefully, will continue to improve. The examples I have given point up the absolute necessity for the government continuing with market research,


improving our selling techniques, ironing out our transportation problems and modernizing our port facilities. If our grading system needs changing to conform to export demands, let us change it. If that means tailoring our grades to meet the protein content demanded by our customers, then by all means let us meet their qualifications and go after their business. All those things must be done if we are to retain our traditional markets and acquire new ones. The western farmer is efficient, versatile, and willing and able to produce; but he is stultified by marketing problems which are beyond his control. He is looking for aggressive action by those in authority who hold the key to the solution of his problems. Is it too much for him to expect that this government will quit vacillating and give some aggressive leadership in providing the solutions to the problems I have outlined.
I have quoted figures related to marketing in order to show how difficult it is for the farmer to resolve his problem of growing indebtedness and cash shortage with a delivery quota of only five or six bushels at the most. Even his repayment of cash advances will be difficult. Despite all this, the minister rose in the House on November 18 and announced a curtailment in federal farm production programs, the phasing out of three experimental farms and a general cutback within his department of assistance programs. This only means that the government, in trying to sell its phony austerity program to the people, has picked agriculture as the most vulnerable scapegoat in order to reduce its research programs, withdraw its services to the farming communities and reduce even its meagre cash outlay to the 4H clubs where thousands of young Canadians are being taught good citizenship through a largely volunteer teaching program.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, we are glad that the minister has been able to persuade the government to recognize, even to the extent of the provision of this bill, that western Canada faces problems the solutions of which depend to a large extent on the actions of this governement. I know that the minister, as a westerner, has been aware of these problems ever since he assumed responsibility for his portfolio. Is it too much to expect that the government, having taken this first hesitant step, will begin to show some leadership in this regard and develop programs that will allow the rural areas of this nation to participate in the so-called just society.
December 5, 1969

Mr. Chairman, may I first express my deep appreciation to the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley who permitted me to speak in his place. He was to have spoken at this time but because I have to attend the funeral of Mr. Andy Fairnie who for fifty years was a valued servant of the Crown and to members of this House. The hon. member very kindly agreed that I might have the opportunity to attend that funeral, and I appreciate very much his courtesy.
Hear, hear.

This legislation naturally receives our support. I think that the hon. member for Lisgar covered the situation exceptionally well in his speech. Having a wide knowledge of farming and having held a high position within his province in the agricultural field, the hon. member has spoken with that ability which experience has enabled him to do.
We support this legislation. The administration which I had the honour of leading as Prime Minister supported the idea of legislation involving cash advances. For many years while in opposition we tried to have it brought in, but the government said it could not be done. What was regarded as heresy when first introduced by the administration in 1957 has now become orthodoxy and a means whereby assistance is to be made available to the western farmer. Repentance is always appreciated, however long delayed. The situation on the prairies is very serious. In the province of Saskatchewan the crop on almost 1 million acres is unthreshed. Those farmers find themselves in a disastrous position.
On December 2, as reported at page 1479 of Hansard, I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Humboldt. Mr. Speaker said that he objected to the form of the question, and I said that I did not know how to bring the matter to the minister's attention except by telling him what took place. The Canadian Wheat Board-and indirectly Saskatoon-Humboldt MP Otto Lang, minister in charge-took it on the chin again Friday from Saskatchewan farmers.
This time the punches came from delegates at the Saskatchewan Liberal Association's panel discussion on wheat. They covered the field from the wheat board and box car shortage to sagging international sales, in an attempt to pin down the reasons for the current wheat sales crisis in Saskatchewan.

About all western Canada ever gets from him is a bow. See what you can do. Let me read on:
I will be your advocate for good causes. The special arguments for a fair deal for agriculture have never been understood in eastern Canada. As your member I would campaign in the streets of Ontario and Quebec as well as with parliament and cabinet to show these people what justice for agriculture means.
I know the minister is bona fide in his determination. I suggest he should get behind some of the ideas that are being put forward for the benefit of western Canada, and in particular agriculture.
They have never understood.
That statement refers to the people of Ontario and Quebec.
They think we want subsidies or welfare. They must learn that simple justice demands a better deal for the farmer and fixed income groups. These people have no control over their incomes but buy goods in a world where most prices are fixed to assure the supplier a good income. We have given these suppliers control over their prices but we have done nothing to protect the farmer and pensioner. Correcting this wrong will be my first priority.
Hear, hear.

That was applause from some of the minister's colleagues. I only hope the minister can convert them because up to the present time they have shown no sign of doing anything. Nothing effective has been done since the month of June, 1968 to help

the serious situation in western Canada. I am glad to have that declaration of independence on the part of the minister. I am glad to learn of the resounding words in which he is going to speak out. I would like to see him start. I read his speeches. They are well put together; his diction is perfection itself, but what action is there in the end? What does the heading say? "Action Lang".
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should go to work now and start parading the streets of Ontario and Quebec. But before he does that, he should start on the cabinet to see if he can get some action concerning this serious situation which has never been equalled, not only in western Canada but Canada as a whole. One and a half billion bushels of grain are piled up. What has occurred in consequence of that pile-up is that the pipelines are entirely or virtually closed. We have to get the wheat out of the line elevators. We have to clear the pipelines. That means some tremendous action must be taken, otherwise the farmers cannot sell their wheat. There is no opportunity of moving it, no matter what the transportation facilities might be.
I suggest the government must take effective means without delay to bring about in western Canada a storage system similar to that in the United States and construct what are called Butler bins. They are made of metal and hold up to 50,000 bushels each. The government will have to make available in western Canada, for the assistance of western farmers, facilities of that kind in order to clear the pipeline so there will be available space.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Lisgar dealt with certain phases of statistics. The minister, in one of his recent releases dated December 1, warned that farmers may have to reduce wheat acreage. He stressed that, through the efforts of the Canadian Wheat Board, Canada has maintained its share of the world market in the face of stiff international competition. That is the story that is being told all over western Canada. It is not true. That is simple and unadulterated fiction for political purposes.
I intend to place on the record the situation with respect to Canada's share of world trade, specifically restricting it to wheat, unless the House wishes to know the record so far as

oats and barley are concerned, since 1957-58. In the first year that we were in office, Canada increased her percentage from the preceding year, and equalled the year 195556, with 30 per cent of the world market. In 1962-63, the last year that we were in office, the amount had gone down. For 1963-64, following the last year we were in office, the percentage was 29 per cent. In other words, we are losing our share of the world market. This can only be the result of the failure of the government to get behind the Wheat Board. In order to keep the record clear-I have given all the statistics-I will take oats. In our first year, we had 23 per cent of the world's trade. They are from the FAO world grain statistics and also from the publication, "Canadian Exports, Wheat, Oats and Barley". We would not be in the position we are today if the minister had carried out the intention he expressed during the course of the election when he said there was a disinterest in the situation in western Canada which he intended to rectify.
What about the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? He has an affable way of saying nothing. He never did a more effective job than on December 4 when I asked him a very simple question having to do with the European Common Market. Oh, I can read. I asked:
With the admission of Great Britain to the European Common Market, will Canada, Australia and New Zealand he reasonably protected by assurance of the British government against a serious diminution in the amount of their exports of agricultural and other products to the United Kingdom.
About nine lines later in the record, the minister said:
The British government has assured us of its readiness to keep us informed as developments occur in the present round of negotiations.
The question did not ask whether Canada was being kept informed. It was: Have you secured an undertaking? Have you tried? The answer is that hon. gentlemen opposite have not tried, or, at least, they had not tried up to the day before yesterday. If they have done so in the last two days, that is their first effort. The minister went on to say:
We expect that the U.K. and ECM, both important trading partners with Canada, will take Canada's interests into account. As a matter of fact, we hope the entry of the U.K. will mark a further liberalization of EEC policies especially with respect to agricultural products and non-tariff barriers.
There is no basis whatever for that statement. It is simply an expression of a pious hope which cannot be achieved. I again come back to the question I raised earlier.
Will the minister now answer the question whether or not the United Kingdom has given any assurance similar to the assurance given by the MacMillan government in 1960 and 1961 that if Great Britain entered the European Common Market Canada's wheat exports, as well as agricultural exports from other parts of the Commonwealth would be, as far as possible, protected and assured before entry into the European Common Market would be acceptable to the United Kingdom?
What was the minister's answer?
That could be, in my view, a denial of the postulate accepted by the right hon. gentleman, which is the right of England to go its own way. However, I would think that in its own interests the United Kingdom would be mindful of our interests.
Mr. Chairman, there never was in six lines more nonsense encompassed.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to state that this party supports the principle behind this cash advance legislation. We feel there is an obvious need for some additional cash to be put in the hands of the farmers. Since the farmers must operate in an uncontrolled environment, particularly in some sections of the prairies, and since they cannot control prices and the cost of
[The Chairman.]

operating their farms-at the present time they are not able to make up their loss by increasing their volume of sales-it is essential just to keep them in business that they receive some cash immediately to carry them over on a short term basis until something further can be done to improve their situation.
With regard to the situation on the prairies as I see it, I should like to emphasize that while a cash advance is a beneficial measure for the government to enact, we are really only postponing the inevitable. The day of reckoning will come. What is really required are larger grain sales or some other way of injecting cash into the prairie economy. In this regard, I am aware that the government is hoping that something will emerge to get them off the hook, so to speak.
However, may I suggest to the Minister without Portfolio that he take a serious look at what might happen if sales do not increase or the situation is not taken in hand. I am sure the minister is aware that the economy is in trouble, even without these cash advances, and if sales are not obtained we will be in worse trouble. I am not hoping that the government or the minister will be embarrassed as a result, but as a farmer from the prairies I am hoping that markets for grain will be found so as to solve the problems of the farmers in that area. If anything can be done, either to increase grain sales or to enable farmers to switch to some other type of farming operation then I would be in favour of it.
I should like to discuss for a moment the change that has gradually come about in the attitude of several governments in Canada. At one time there was no such thing as a cash advance to farmers. There was then introduced legislation enabling them to obtain loans from the bank at a certain rate of interest. Then the government passed legislation to provide a $3,000 advance interest free, and this amount has now been increased to $6,000. We now have this legislation to advance cash on unthreshed grain. I do not think these several measures conformed to any consistent, over-all plan; like Topsy, they "just growed".
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
While I agree that each of these steps is essential I feel a little uneasy about amendment being piled on amendment without any over-all approach to a solution or program. This government is involved in a number of advances or loans in various forms to the
December 5, 1969
agricultural industry or farmers. These are in the form of guaranteed loans, payments through the Farm Credit Corporation or cash advances. I wonder whether some farmers realize the awkward situation this brings about in respect of proper loan management or adequate sales. I would think this government should take some over-all responsibility by taking a new look at the agricultural policy in an effort to determine where the responsibility of the government lies, where the responsibility of the grain industry lies or where the responsibility of the individual farmer lies. In other words, the government should determine where these three areas of responsibility start and stop.
We feel that the involvement of the government and the farmers of Canada in the GATT agreement is not to the advantage of the Canadian grain industry. I respectfully suggest to the minister that the interests of the primary grains producers in Canada were sacrificed for the interests of those who produce manufactured products. I suggest it is proper that a member from western Canada should have some concern about this. The grain industry has suffered rather than benefited as a result of all the hoopla suggested by the government with regard to the proposed GATT agreement.
Some little time ago, I suggested to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance that we could do with some organization in so far as the handling of grain is concerned. I mentioned, for example, that there were demands at the Lakehead for flax and there was no flax there. Last winter grain sales were available at the west coast and there was no grain there.
I suggest that some better organization within the government departments or on the part of the people who actually handle and manage this grain would be beneficial not only to the grain handlers themselves but to the farmers and the economy of Canada as a whole. I believe the government could be saved considerable political embarrassment if these problems were solved beforehand instead of afterward. I think, too, the farmers would like to know where they stand within the agricultural economy and what is expected of an individual farmer or small businessman within the Canadian economy. Obviously, he cannot go out and sell in the world markets in competition with the governments of other countries. When our Prime Minister stands up in Winnipeg and says, "Why should I sell grain", I suggest this shows that the
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop Prime Minister does not understand the problem in respect of world markets today. It is time someone told him about the actual problem of disposing of grain and grain sales in the world markets. As a farmer, I feel indignant about this. I also feel indignant about it as a representative of the area. I think the same situation is true in respect of any other small business which tries to sell on an international market.
The minister has suggested he intends to look into the question of the improper movement of grains eastward in Canada. In the Star Phoenix for Wednesday, December 3, he is quoted as saying that he will look into reports of improper movement of western feed grains to eastern Canada. I suggest that he look into the matter of the improper movement of feed grains within western Canada as well, because I suggest the government has winked its eye at the transfer of grains across the borders of the three prairie provinces. If it is not a good thing that this grain should move back and forth, then let us police it in order to see that this is not done. If it is a good thing, then let us change the law rather than have the government wink its eye at the infractions.
The Minister without Portfolio from Sas-katoon-Humboldt indicated he would like to be able to say to the farmers in the spring what crops they should grow. He is studying this matter. I should like to make some suggestions to the minister. I would suggest, for example, that the government say to the farmers that it will accept several million bushels of rapeseed over and above the normal public demand, and that it will be prepared to withhold this from the commercial market if there should be a surplus. I suggest the government also say this in connection with several million bushels of flax seed and Durum wheat. A number of times in my farming experience there have been occasions when, because of a market or production collapse in some other countries, we have been able to dispose of several million extra bushels beyond our expectations. For this reason let us have more alternatives. Let us have a supply of the various different grains on hand, but let us not ruin the normal commercial market.
It is better to carry a little extra supply of rapeseed, flax or Durum wheat than to have all our surplus in the form of one type of grain. 1 have one further suggestion for the minister from Saskatoon-Humboldt. I believe there should be a little more promotion in

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, since the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley yielded to the right hon. member for Prince Albert, we are perfectly willing that the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville carry on the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take perhaps 10 or 15 minutes to say a few words in this debate. First of all, I wish to say that I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley who has been involved with farming organizations much longer than I. I find that in my constituency there really is not too much unthreshed grain at the present time, although there are certain small pockets where the farmers do have unthreshed grain. In general, I suppose, only about 2 per cent or 3 per cent of the grain in my constituency would not be threshed at the present moment. This is partly because of what the minister said at the outset of the debate this morning. We have had some fairly good weather in the last month or so and many people, even in the last couple of weeks, have been able to store their grain. But, as was stated already in the House this morning, almost one million acres of grain across the prairies or in Saskatchewan has not yet been threshed. Most of it, of course, is in the most northerly part of the province.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
So I am very happy, at the outset of my speech, to lend my support to this bill. I hope that it will be passed expeditiously, so that the farmers who are in this unfortunate position can obtain some cash as soon as possible to meet some very pressing financial needs.

DEBATES	December 5. 1969
The purpose of the bill is to authorize provisional payments for the 1969-70 crop year in respect of unthreshed grain in the prairie provinces. I think that the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley has already briefly traced the history of this type of legislation by which the minister is helping a number of people in the prairies, and I must commend him for that. We can remember the time when there were no advance payments at all for western farmers. Then, there was an advance payment up to a maximum of $3,000, which was later increased to $6,000 and today we have a bill before us which authorizes advance payments to farmers with unthreshed grain. Under the bill I believe that a farmer can claim up to half of his acreage, regardless of the quality of the grain, and there is a maximum of $3,000 per farmer. The bill says that a farmer can collect up to $1 a bushel on wheat, up to 40 cents a bushel on oats, and I believe that the limit on barley is 70 cents.
While I am on my feet, I cannot help but underline some of the things that have been mentioned by one or two speakers this morning and this afternoon. If we think that cash advances alone will really solve the problem, we are putting off the inevitable and we are disregarding some of the things that will happen. I spent a couple of days last month touring my constituency during which time I was able to get out to many small towns and talk to many of the farmers there. All the stories they told me were pretty well the same. Most of them are faced with severe financial problems which affect not only the farmers but many of the small businessmen, and indeed practically everyone in the prairie region.
I think the minister himself is aware of this situation. The right hon. member for Prince Albert reminded the minister once again this morning of the response he received at the Saskatchewan Liberal convention from many of his fellow Liberals in the province of Saskatchewan. It is not very often that I find myself agreeing with the premier of Saskatchewan, but I think even he is realizing that there are many problems with which the federal government has not been able to cope during their term of office so far. The right hon. member for Prince Albert also spoke about a letter that the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt had sent out to his constituents just before the election in 1968. In that letter he stated a few things which I think were very interesting. He said
December 5, 19G9	COMMONS
that many people in eastern Canada do not really understand the problems which confront the people in the west, particularly with reference to agriculture. He said that he is going to change this and that he, as an individual, will do his utmost to do something about it. He said he was prepared to walk down the streets of Quebec and Ontario in an attempt to change the attitude of people in the east. If I knew this would help I, myself, would walk down the streets with the minister. I am sure many more on this side of the House would join him also.
There is a point that should be taken seriously, and that is that there is a real misunderstanding among many people in eastern Canada, particularly in the cities, of what is happening in western Canada today. Many people think that farmers there are actually fairly wealthy, perhaps because they do have a lot of money tied up in a farming operation of one kind or another. To illustrate this perhaps I can refer to a letter which I received from an elderly gentleman in Windsor last year. This person was writing me a letter after one or two farm debates in the House. He was quite sincere when he said that he had been told that about 85 per cent of Saskatchewan farmers are so well off they go to California or Florida every winter. He wrote that he did not believe this, but he does know that at least 50 per cent of them are sufficiently well off to go to California or Florida in the winter.
As anyone knows, this is just not the case. Of course all of us who are from the west can easily vouch for that fact. But this statement does indicate some of the misunderstandings that many people have of the type of problem with which the farmer finds himself confronted today. As I said, cash advances help to alleviate the immediate problem of many of these people, but they are not the only solution or the only answer. Many people seem to believe that when the government gives out cash advances they are giving the farmers money. This is not the case. Those are just advances on the money that the farmers will obtain once they sell their grain, following which these loans will be repaid.
Perhaps I can spend one or two minutes going into some of the things that are happening out west so that some hon. members may understand more readily why the situation is serious, and why it will become more and more serious in the near future. I think there is no doubt that conditions are going
DEBATES	1653
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop from bad to worse and that farmers have their backs to the wall. For example, in 196869 Saskatchewan farmers were able to market on the average less than five bushels of wheat per acre. At this rate, even the most efficient of farmers cannot hope to begin to meet his production costs. Many farmers say that the average production cost per acre in Saskatchewan, when you take everything into consideration, is about $21 per acre. Meanwhile, the average income per acre in the last year was $8.09. So the cost was $21, and the income was $8. As you can see, not even the most efficient farmer can hope to meet expenses when conditions are this difficult for them.
This situation does not only affect farmers. As I said at the outset, it affects almost everyone in Saskatchewan. All you have to do is to go to any small town in Saskatchewan and talk to people on the main streets, people who own businesses. First, you will notice that farm machinery dealers are going bankrupt or are pulling out in many of the small towns across the prairies. I believe that last year farm machinery sales were down by over 20 per cent in the province of Saskatchewan. I know that housing starts were down by 20 per cent in the province. So, the situation affects everyone because, regardless of what you do when you live in a province such as Saskatchewan and particularly in an area such as mine, you are indirectly affected by everything that affects farmers. Your own welfare is directly correlated to that of the farmers.
We may ask ourselves whether the government is aware of what is happening in the west today. I maintain they are. There are three ministers from western Canada in the cabinet: the minister who is presenting the bill before us, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Supply and Services. In addition, all three provincial governments in the prairies have made representations to the federal government, and once again this was done at the recent Liberal convention in Saskatchewan a week or two ago. Then, too, opposition parties in this House have been asking the government questions every second day and have been offering them ideas as well as bringing the situation to their attention. This has not only been done by the opposition parties. I know that many government members, such as the hon. member for Assiniboia, have been drawing the government's attention to problems facing people in western Canada.

Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop [DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Perhaps even more important is the fact that, many farm organizations have presented briefs and have met members of the cabinet and members of the government party. I am referring here to the National Farmers' Union and its provincial members. I am talking about the Wheat Pool. I am talking about the Federation of Agriculture and other agricultural organizations across the country. All of us remember that the Standing Committee on Agriculture, which was composed of members of all political parties, made a tour of the west last session. The Committee members talked to the people and toured the farms. They heard briefs. Then, the Committee made a number of recommendations, many of which I believe hon. members have said have been ignored by the government.
Now, we can say that the government is certainly aware of what is happening in western Canada. Last July the Prime Minister went to Regina and Saskatoon to, in his own words, find out what was going on and to hear from the farmers themselves what their problems were. I think he found out. What happened in Saskatchewan last July may only be the beginning if something is not done, and done immediately, to alleviate the crisis facing western agriculture. I suggest that the government has done very little. I support the bill before us today to provide cash advances, but this serves only a very limited purpose. We must get some money into the western economy as soon as possible. We must sell grain. We must move the grain we do have as fast as possible, and store as much as possible in terminals and elevators so that the farmers can have some cash in their pockets as soon as possible.
I know that during the last two or three days the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has been trying to get some answers from the Minister without Portfolio from Sas-katoon-Humboldt on the storage of grain. He has been asking questions about the National Harbours Board terminal, No. 2, in Vancouver. He has been asking why it has been empty for about a year. From the information in our possession, we know that if the terminal were repaired it could be used for the storage of grain, for the loading and unloading of grain. It could be used for the storage of rapeseed, flax, and certain grades of wheat. I believe it could be repaired quite cheaply. I believe this must be done, because it would be very irresponsible not to do all that is pos-

sible to get as much grain as possible off the farms. When the minister is replying I hope he can offer us a few comments on this National Harbours Board terminal in Vancouver, and tell us what the situation is right now as well as what the government intends to do about it. I believe the capacity of this terminal is 1,200,000 bushels. It is sitting there empty. If we can fix it up and store grain in it, this would be much appreciated by the farmers in western Canada.
Another point I would like to discuss with the minister at this time, and I do so once again because I think it would lessen the need for cash advances or maybe help farmers repay some of the advances they are going to get, is the proposal put forward in a resolution passed just last week-end in Saskatoon by the Farmers Union of the province of Saskatchewan. They suggested a moratorium on the repayment of many types of farm debts, debts owing to the Farm Credit Corporation, and Farm Improvement Loans. Such a moratorium would provide legal authorization to defer repayments. I am not sure how long repayments should be deferred. This is something we cannot decide at the present time, but we should do it for perhaps a year or two, at least until the farmers in western Canada do have some grain that can be sold. I suggest to the minister that the government should seriously consider imposing a moratorium on both interest rates and loans for a certain period of time. If this is not done, and grain is not sold so that cash will be put into the western economy, many farmers will go bankrupt. I do not think I am exaggerating the case. I hear this story all the time as I travel through my constituency.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, summing up as quickly as I can, I think the government must realize it has to make a number of radical changes in its attitude toward agriculture generally. The farmer must have some guarantee of the price he is going to get for his commodity. He must have a better idea of what he can produce and sell. The farmer's income is constantly fluctuating. He never knows what he is going to get for a product, or how much it will cost him to produce a product. He never knows what to produce and, in part, the fault for this situation lies with the federal government. I think we can safely say that the farmer has been led astray many times on the question of whether he should grow wheat or other grains. The Prime Minister, when he was campaigning in Winnipeg in June, 1968, told the farmers that
December 5, 1969	COMMONS
they should grow as much wheat as they possibly could because the government would sell it. But a few months later, also in Winnipeg, he asked them, "Why should I sell your grain? I cannot do it. After all, I am only the Prime Minister of this country." I, for one, cannot tolerate this type of irresponsibility on the part of somebody who holds the position of Prime Minister of this country. Apart from all this, we must do a number of new things to try to keep farm costs down, costs that have been going up by leaps and bounds during the last four or five years.
In summation, Mr. Chairman, the situation is very serious and I hope that in some way over the next few months I can re-emphasize this as strongly as possible. I think the type of thing we saw in Saskatchewan last July is only the beginning of something that is going to become much worse unless the government does something. Cash advances are helping right now, but they are just a housekeeping measure and will not solve the problem. When the minister replies I hope he will comment on one or two of the suggestions I have put forward this afternoon. With that, Mr. Chairman, I resume my seat, and ask members of the House to pass this bill as quickly as possible so that we can get a little cash into the hands of some farmers who were not able to harvest their grain this fall.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak briefly on this bill. I believe it is a good bill, the provisions of which will be of great benefit to those unfortunate farmers who have been able to harvest little or no grain this fall. Some time ago I suggested to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board that it would not be necessary to send this bill to the Standing Committee on Agriculture and that it would be preferable, in the interests of speedy action, to have it dealt with as rapidly as possible in the House of Commons itself. I am glad that this is the procedure that has been adopted.
I was hoping this measure could have taken the form of permanent legislation which would be available any year in the future when a similar need might develop. However, we farmers are eternal optimists, and we can always hope that we will not soon have a repetition of the adverse harvest weather experienced in many parts of the prairies this fall. As the minister pointed out, there has been some harvesting done in western
DEBATES	1655
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop Canada in the past few days because of unusually good weather, which saw new records set for high temperatures at various localities in recent days.
I was also hoping that there would have been an amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act to take care of an anomaly that has developed as a result of the deferred delivery plan. Those unfortunate farmers who were not given an opportunity to deliver the promised five-bushel quota during the crop year which ended last July 31 have been authorized to carry forward that quota and sell it this year. Many of those farmers had no outstanding cash advances on July 31, but because they desperately needed money they took cash advances after August 1. Now, when they deliver grain on their deferred authorizations, half of the proceeds are deducted to be applied in the new cash advances.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
If they had been treated equitably last summer they would have received the full amount for their grain. Now, they are being given further unfair treatment. Not only have these farmers had their income delayed several months, but they have had to accept an initial payment 20 cents less than they would have received last July. They have also been faced with a proportionately greater storage problem this fall than their more fortunate fellow farmers who were able to deliver their five bushels in 1968-69. Now they are encountering this further discrimination, and many of them are justifiably incensed. In the long run it will not make a great deal of difference, since all farmers hope to fully repay these advances, but with the present cash shortage it is a very significant item to those farmers affected. It is probably too late now to correct this inequity, but I hope the minister will take it into consideration.
My mail continues to be liberally sprinkled with letters complaining about unfair distribution of box cars for grain. Many of them are coming from farmers who are in the "block system" of box car control. These complaints bear out my previously stated contention that the "block system" was not designed to provide even distribution of box cars as between points and as between producers. Its main aim is to make more efficient use of our grain gathering, transporting, and handling systems, to the end that the right grain will be at the right place at the right time. This
1656	COMMONS
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop will better service our customers, and maximize our sales, wherein lies the main hope to revive our ailing grain industry.
I believe the "block system", which is designed to call forward only those grains in current demand, will leave thousands of farmers with little or no opportunity to deliver unwanted grain which they have as a result of weather and other conditions beyond their control. Therefore, I suggest that what is required soon is a massive extension of the cash advances system whereby farmers will be paid a large percentage of the value of an authorized quota of grain, whether or not they can deliver it, and whereby those farmers who are forced to retain the grain on the farm will be compensated for storing it. They should be paid for the full authorized quota with no arbitrary ceiling, except perhaps a hold-back of about 10 per cent of the value to insure delivery when the grain is required.
Speaking of quotas, I must say that there is much dissatisfaction with the operation of the quota system. This has been evident for many years, and I could produce correspondence I had with the Wheat Board in this regard several years ago. When the Wheat Board members appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture last spring, I suggested that the quota system needed revising. The Chief Commissioner agreed that it did, but showed no disposition at that time to go into the matter and apparently nothing was done. After the federal government appointed Mr. Charles Gibbings to the Wheat Board on July 1, 1969-a very commendable appointment in my opinion and in the opinion of every farmer I have talked with since-I sent my suggestions about quota revision to him. A few weeks later I was very pleased to have a reply from him indicating that the Wheat Board had set up an internal committee to review quota policy and recommend appropriate modifications. I look forward to the results of this study with great anticipation.
It is interesting to note how different people use statistics in different ways. The right hon. member for Prince Albert produced some statistics to show that the percentage of world wheat trade Canada has enjoyed, has varied from time to time. I believe that the total number of bushels sold is of more significance to farmers than percentages. According to figures published in the papers prepared for the Canadian Agricultural Outlook Conference, which was held here in Ottawa last week, Canada's exports of wheat in the five-year

DEBATES	December 5, 1969
period 1958-1962, the Diefenbaker-Hamilton years, averaged 315.7 million bushels per year. In the next five years, 1963-1967 wheat exports averaged 483.2 million bushels per year, up over 50 per cent. During the past two crop years, which ended on July 31, 1968 and July 31, 1969, Canada's wheat exports averaged 320.6 million bushels, a little higher than the period from 1958 to 1962. I will agree those figures are far from satisfactory but, as all hon. members know, there is some prospect of improvement, certainly over the longer term. The efforts of the Canada Grains Council, and the new grains group under the direction of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, which he announced in a press conference this morning, will soon pay off in greater wheat sales, and better management of our grain economy generally, I am sure.
Before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment but briefly on two more items. First, some opposition spokesmen have been critical of the government because the legislation was not presented earlier. I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that in a similar situation ten years ago, but under the government headed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, legislation to authorize cash advances on unthreshed grain was not passed by Parliament until January of the following year.
Second, I want to correct the false impression the right hon. member for Prince Albert tried to leave about what happened at the Saskatchewan Liberal convention last week in Saskatoon. It is true that a small number of delegates complained about some operations and decisions of the Wheat Board. This is not unusual, because farmers have complained about various aspects of the Wheat Board operation for years. This is very understandable because of the all-pervading influence of the Wheat Board on almost every farmer. Regulations developed for general application do not always meet the desires of all farmers everywhere. It would be strange indeed if every one was completely satisfied with the operation of that Board. The important thing is that when a lengthy resolution, critical of the Wheat Board, was presented to the full convention, it was enthusiastically and almost unanimously turned down by the delegates, after a spirited defence of the Wheat Board by the federal Minister of Agriculture.
As I said in a previous speech during this session, the Liberal party is fully committed to the Wheat Board system of orderly mar-
December 5, 1969	COMMONS
keting, and we are developing plans to improve it and make it even more satisfactory to the farmers concerned. I could talk about a wide variety of other subjects, as some of the other speakers have done, but I have tried to confine my remarks to arguments raised by previous speakers, and to questions related to Bill C-157, the Prairie Grain Provisional Payments Act. I hope it is passed this afternoon, and that it will be quickly brought into operation.
Tell us about the odd balls.

Mr. Chairman, it is not only my privilege but my duty to rise at this time to present my views on Bill C-157, an act to authorize provisional payments for the 196970 crop year in respect of unthreshed grain in the prairie provinces. I was happy to join with other members and parties in the House to send this bill directly to the committee of the whole house, rather than the Standing Committee on Agriculture, in order to speed up its passage and provide some emergency help for hard-pressed prairie farmers.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I must hasten to say that I am pleased the government has finally decided, after many strong recommendations by the opposition, to move at least in some small way towards bringing some assistance to our hard-pressed western farmers. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that in 1958 a situation similar to the one prevailing now obtained in western Canada. There was a major pile-up of grain on western farms. Not only farmers' bins and all elevators, but skating rinks as well were stocked to capacity with grain. Accordingly, a payment of $2 per acre was provided in 1958. In 1959 we had a major snow storm early in the fall, with the result that western farmers could not harvest their crops. A further acreage payment was provided at that time. Then, in 1961 we witnessed another of nature's vicissitudes when we experienced one of the worst droughts in Canada's history. A further acreage payment was provided, the total of the three acreage payments being altogether $325 million.
At present in western Canada there is want, so to speak, in a land of plenty. Our very successful farmers are sitting on huge grain surpluses for which there is no market. Those farmers have bills to pay which are almost double what they were 12 years ago. As a result of inflation in Canada, largely brought on by policies of the present government as well as by wage settlements that followed the Pearson formula, prices have risen to the extent that it costs a farmer double what it cost him 10 or 12 years ago to produce a bushel of grain. That is why I have suggested a payment of $2 an acre up to a maximum of 400 acres. The task force on agriculture recommended last spring that, in view of the pile-up of grain in the west, it would be better if we cut back on wheat growing or grain growing over the next ten years until the situation becomes stabilized. That may be good advice.
Nevertheless, it will be difficult for farmers to abandon crops yielding ready cash. To what will they turn? The raising of beef stock has been suggested. Also, it has been suggested that western farmers could raise pork as a temporary, emergency measure, in order to tide them overt these difficult times. Knowing something about the life cycle of pigs, I content that within a short period we should see over-production of pork. The long term answer to stabilizing our agricultural industry is for our farmers to diversify, and raise products like beef. Some say that if we do that, we should very soon see an overabundance of beef.

The fascinating thing is that there is more than one group. There is a grains council now meeting. It was intended that this body would make recommendations to the government.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
An agricultural task force is meeting and considering these problems, and it will be making recommendations. Apparently the group under the hon. gentleman will hear representations, will ponder and reflect on them, and probably years from now the group will come to some decision. The minister does not need a group. He has been hearing from the group on this side of the House precisely what are the things which need to be done, how they can be done and when they should be done. I suggest that this new group represents just another procrastination. This government is planning task force upon task force, group upon group, procrastination and delay. This is the kind of thing which in western Canada has become the byword of this government, and I am sure the minister found that out on a recent occasion in Saskatchewan at a meeting of those few Liberals in the province who are still bold enough to admit they carry that title.
