It has been said that this is not bad legislation. We have been asking for it, among other things. The minister himself said today in his speech that the farmers' record of repayment is excellent. I confirm that. The minister said that the bill does not add to the expenditures of the government except in a minimal way. I think the hon. member for Gaspe had some doubts about this legislation. He should have listened to the minister who said that this measure will cost the government only a small amount of money.
Although there are one or two questions which we will want to ask when we come to the appropriate clause, let me state in general that this bill does not meet the needs and demands of areas such as my constituency and many areas of northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan. The Minister of Agriculture ventured into the Peace River country some two weeks ago on a 1J- or two-day trip. He stopped at a number of
DEBATES	1665
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop points for a few minutes and listened to representations by farmers, businessmen and farm organizations.
There is no excuse for this government saying it is not aware of the problems in northern Alberta. In 1965, because of difficult conditions such as too much rain at the wrong time and frost which came too early, the crop was almost a complete disaster. At that time I made representations to the then minister of agriculture, now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who was good enough to indicate that he was interested in the problem. I asked him what he could do about it. The provincial government intimated it would be prepared to make some expenditures and it offered some money to the farmers. I asked the minister, "Are you prepared to make arrangements for compensation to be made available to these people?"
The minister went to the then minister of finance, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who said "No", just as he said "No" earlier this year to the people of Biafra. In 1967 we had the worst drought in the history of the northern part of the country. In 1968 the quality of the crop was very bad because of early frost, and in 1969 we also have problems. I say to the committee that a great many farmers in that area will not be able to survive this winter. A few weeks ago there was no hope of harvesting a million acres in the Peace River country alone. Since then I have heard stories concerning damage done by fieldmice which are depreciating the quality of the grain which is left there.
If it is the intention of the government, as I suspect it is, to try to shove farmers off the land, do nothing to help them and push them into the cities to add to the problems of urban dwellers, increasing the pressure on housing and adding to the problems of the already crowded cities, they are going about it in the right way. This is precisely the feeling we have in the north country regarding the intentions of this government. In fact it is saying, "Get off the land; go into the cities and be looked after there." This is not the time and place to argue about the stupidity of such a policy, but I think we can all agree that it is stupid.
What can be done? We have heard suggestions from different parts of the House. I support some of them, and I have other suggestions. Today I introduced a private member's public bill on amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. The amount of money which will be available under this
December 5, 1969
1666	COMMONS
Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop legislation will not be enough in many instances to do more than pay interest charges on land and machinery, to pay for fuel, harvesting and seeding in the spring, or to pay taxes; far less will it maintain in a very limited way the farmer and his family during the summer, the ensuing winter and until next harvest.
In order for most of these people to be retained on the land as good and effective producers, cash payments must be given to them and some arrangement made to protect them against debt. I challenged the Minister of Agriculture on this earlier and he said the federal government had no jurisdiction in the matter. That is not a correct statement of fact. Jurisdiction in this regard does lie with the federal government. In 1934, under the Conservative government, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed. It provided for the reduction of debts to a point where it was possible for farmers to meet them when payment fell due. It provided for the reduction of interest rates and for orderly payment over a period of time-
The private members' public bill which I introduced today provides for that program and it provides that the government may introduce it in areas in which it is required.
I know there are many instances today where foreclosure action is being commenced, although it is not as widespread as may be the case later because I think there are creditors who have a conscience and take a reasonable approach to the problem. But I know that a number of seizures of machinery and equipment are being made by finance companies, and there are a number of related actions.
The effect is that the court costs and the interest involved which the farmer will have to cover will minimize the payments envisaged under the act so that they will not do the farmer any good. He will be faced with an increased amount of debt and will be unable to meet his obligations when they fall due. So the government must be prepared, if necessary in collaboration with provincial governments, to say to the creditors who are making exorbitant and unconscionable demands in attempting to extract from farmers payments which they cannot make, "If you insist on this action, we have the right, through the exercise of such legislative proposals as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, to stop it." I think the government will not be accepting its responsibility if it is not prepared to do that.


Second, acreage payments must be made to farmers. What is being given by this bill is not a gift; it is simply an advance on what farmers will receive in any event. The minister said it will not cost the government anything. I suggest that some arrangement in this regard must be made in collaboration with the provincial governments. I understand that the provincial government in Alberta indicated its willingness to negotiate in this respect and I would like the minister to find out whether that is correct. Acreage payments must be made. They are by reason of previous experience. The Conservative government under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert did this on two or three occasions, and it was very effective and useful.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Third, some arrangement must be made for the payment of storage on farm-stored grain. In certain instances, with the elevators filled, I say that the licence to operate elevators is simply, as Lord Thomson said about television, a licence to print and make money. There is a good case to be made for doing this under careful scrutiny, because we must bear in mind some of the difficult experiences in the United States with payments to some farmers there for farm-stored grain.
This morning I asked a question of the Minister of Finance, who has been busy going around the country defending the undefendable white paper. I referred to a statement made by the Purchasing Management Association of Canada, that 60 per cent of the businesses surveyed expected higher prices and production levels in 1970. What chance has a farmer living in the northern part of Alberta or Saskatchewan, under the circumstances I have described, to make a living and survive?
There must be protection. There must be an opportunity for these people to be kept on the land, to become effective, useful, good producers. That would be better than to have them yanked off their land and pushed into cities, in many cases to be the object of welfare payments and assistance at a cost infinitely greater than would be the cost of keeping them on the land as potential producers.
I suggest to the government that it has not looked at the situation in western Canada. It has no conscience. It does not understand, and does not want to understand, the problems there. The government must understand it has a responsibility to deal with them. This may be one of the measures by which history
December 5. 1969	COMMONS
will judge the government, that is, the extent to which it meets the crisis which exists.

Mr. Chairman, my purpose in speaking on this bill is not to criticize it but only to point out that it is not a cure-all for the present situation. Certainly the bill is necessary to provide some temporary relief for a critical situation, a situation so critical that I make no apology if I use some of the arguments that have already been used by my colleagues; some of them bear repeating.
What is this critical situation, Mr. Chairman, especially in the northern part of the prairie provinces? I have seen this situation myself, so I think I know whereof I speak. Some crops are ten inches under snow, following rains which made the fields too wet to use heavy harvesting machinery. I have seen places where the grain itself was comparatively dry but a combine was stuck before it got nicely started.
I am sure many hon. members saw the picture on the front page of the Montreal Gazette the other day showing nine combines, in a field north of Calgary, harvesting wheat in December. At first glance that is a wonderful thing that combining is being done, but I point out that north of Calgary is not northern or central Alberta or northern Saskatchewan. This was an isolated case, and the government should not have too much hope that the problem will disappear. The combining to which I refer was probably carried out on high, sandy land and only points out what conditions have been like up to this time, because such a field north of Calgary should have been harvested months ago.
I saw combines taken into a field last fall when the ground was drying, but the moisture content of the grain was over 20 per cent and the people concerned were afraid it would not keep. Many farmers, knowing that wheat sales were lost last year, and especially barley sales, would like to know what hope there is for selling their wheat in future. What hope have the farmers of repaying these cash advances? Who knows what further deterioration will take place in the grain during the winter? Losses will occur from mice, sprouting, discoloration, threshing out, and lowering of grades, to mention just a few causes. What if we have a wet spring, or a late spring? What if we have both? What will be the bushel per acre quota? How much grain can the market absorb? Markets are the long-range solution, but what is wrong with acreage payments? Would not this be an equitable

There has been talk of diversification but there has been no direction from the government as to the type of diversification in which farmers should engage. Are farmers to switch to dairying? Certainly we have a surplus of dairy production in eastern Canada. We do not have a surplus in western Canada, yet farmers out there know that the subsidy quotas given to eastern dairymen were originally western quotas. As recently as November 18 last the Minister of Agriculture announced cut-backs in dairy supports. Are farmers going to switch to hog production? It does not take very long to start a hog operation, but what may be the result? The bottom can fall out of the market in a hurry. Remember, there is also going to be a reduction in hog premiums.
What about cattle? As has already been said this afternoon, no switch can be made to beef cattle. It takes years to increase cattle herds to any great extent. What about eggs? We need not spend long on that subject because egg marketing for profit has in most cases always been hopeless in western Canada.
Again speaking of acreage payments, Mr. Chairman, the government seems worried about the cost involved. I believe the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean mentioned this factor. But this is a little difficult to explain to farmers, especially those in areas where crops cannot be harvested. It is difficult to explain to them how the government can find hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on writing off the Expo debt-I might say, at a time when grants to small agricultural fairs are to be curtailed-on hydrofoils, on the Bonaventure, on the CBC, and $40 million for an arts centre serving one city, but no money is available to save a basic industry in time of emergency. All the farmers can look forward to is greater tax burdens, one piled on top of the other.
The proposed centralization of the grain collecting system, about which my colleague the hon. member for Peace River spoke so well, may solve some problems; but it will not solve the problems of the growers. It may even cost them more for hauling. The hon. member for Assiniboia, whom I hope is a good friend of mine, read some figures into the record on grain sales during the eras of different governments. This was supposed to pertain to the problem under discussion today. I think he should point out to the

Mr. Chairman, it is not my duty nor my intention to unduly delay the passage of this bill, but when we look over the Throne Speech we find very little opportunity to voice our opinions on the crisis in agriculture and particularly the economic plight of the west. When we look at the list of proposed legislation we see very little to come before the House of Commons to deal with the serious situation which exists with respect to agriculture in western Canada.
Let me say at the outset that I am in favour of the proposal before us but I am not particularly happy with it. I am not happy with it because it is merely a stopgap meas-


ure designed to take the heat off the government rather than to assist western agriculture. I am not happy with it because it does not get to the root of the problems besetting the whole economy of the west, and in particular the economy of the great agricultural industry. The measure does nothing to solve the desperate shortage of feed, straw, roughage and hay in the northern part of the province of Alberta. Many farmers have already been forced to dispose of herds because of lack of feed and lack of money with which to purchase feed for the winter. There is nothing in the measure to provide for the actual losses that will occur due to the grain lying out in the field during the winter; there is nothing in it to allow for deterioration in the grade.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is rather outdated, outmoded and has become a practically useless tool which is simply adding to the cost of production. The present crop insurance program is not proving to be very effective. As a matter of fact, I think if one took a survey of the average farmer in western Canada, one would find that there is a great deal of indifference toward the administration of that program and, above all, some people feel it adds greatly to the cost of production of a commodity which is declining in value under this administration.
Added to the adversities of weather, marketing, etc., is the daily struggle to get by, and now a cut-back in dairy subsidies and a reallocation of quotas has been announced, causing another slap in the face to the economy of western farmers. These are the people who actually put the bread and butter on the table.
It is true that a more generous scale of advances for farm-stored grain, whether in the bin or still in the field, are necessary and will help to banish the grim shadow of debt and bankruptcy presently lying across so many prairie grain producers. At the same time, it will tend to lock the western grain producer into a system that all the experts and members of this government keep telling him is wrong and is the basis of all his economic woe. What does a more generous scale of economic advances really mean? It means that the farmer will be able to pay off some of his debt to the fertilizer company, the farm machinery dealer, the oil and gas dealer and all those concerned with the agricultural business and maintenance of his farm. It will probably place him in a position in which he can keep going for another year even though

he will still be operating in debt without much prospect of significantly improving his economic status.
Unlike the CNR, the farmer does not have the opportunity of coming to Parliament and asking for millions of dollars to maintain his operation. The government will do nothing to relieve him of the economic cycle that is slowly but surely driving him off the land, out of a once flourishing agricultural community and into the city where he will add to the numerous unskilled labourers already there. This morning we received the latest news summary from the Department of Agriculture, which reports a grim situation. The summary is dated December 5, and states:
Agricultural economists say that total cash receipts will be down about $100 million this year, but expenses will be up 3.5 per cent.
That means that realized net farm income, will be down about 10 per cent from last year to $1,425 million with the tightest pinch being felt in Saskatchewan where the dependence on grain crops is greatest.
Despite the optimism of the hon. member for Assiniboia about the future of the wheat marketing picture, the Department of Agriculture suggests that the outlook continues to be grim, because it states:
The surplus will continue to grow, pushed upward by this year's 685 million bushel crop. At the end of the crop year on July 31, 1970, we'll have more than a billion bushels of wheat on hand, setting a record.
I have spoken before in this House about what I believe to be the considered policy of this government-the writing off of all Canadians who seek to remain small economic units and preserve the family farm. I have also mentioned before that I believe it is the policy of this government to deliberately let Canadian agriculture go to pot as an industry and to destroy our rural way of life.
The Canadian agricultural community has been declared surplus and expendable by this government. This is made amply clear by its lack of a national agricultural policy, the legislation passed last session in relation to estate taxation and now, even more clearly, in the policies on taxation proposed in the white paper of the Minister of Finance.
I suppose this explains why we have had no comprehensive, long-range, practical plan from the government to convert Canadian agriculture into a strong, competitive industry in step with world conditions now prevailing. This is why we in western Canada are being forced to experience the slow and painful

Every measure so far advanced by this government in relation to agriculture, including the one we are now considering, has been an emergency measure to quieten the western cries of protest. There has been a stubborn refusal to act by all the ministers concerned, including the Prime Minister.
I suggest that we must first resolve to preserve the agricultural industry as a vital and necessary part of Canadian society and as an essential sector of the Canadian economy. Once this has been resolved, the next step should be to relate Canadian agricultural production to the domestic and export markets as they exist today, not as they existed years ago when most of our basic agricultural legislation was designed. I think, for instance, that we should completely and radically re-think and re-do our machinery for distributing and marketing. I had the opportunity to attend the United Nations a week ago and whilst there discussed the situation with many of the ambassadors from other parts of the world who are also gravely concerned about wheat marketing. It was suggested that we must revamp our system of grading, and I am very pleased to learn of the proposed amendments to the grain act so that we can be flexible in this regard. Our becoming flexible means that we shall become more competitive, but that will not improve the situation of our farmers financially.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I also think we should take a long-term, comprehensive look at the idea of storing our grain in the countries to whom we sell. It seems that some countries have lost confidence in Canada's ability to distribute the grain that has been sold. We have ample evidence of the loss of confidence which resulted from the bottleneck crisis we experienced last year in Vancouver. Any changes that are instituted should be approached on a truly national basis by considering the public good to be achieved by tying together modern forms of transportation and merchandising and marketing to the sophisticated and ultramodern techniques which have become commonplace on today's farms.
I, too, would like to see the minister launch an investigation into the costs of handling and distributing grain. A number of hon. members touched on this subject, which is worthy of consideration. Certainly, scientific farming in Canada is a reality. We are in the forefront of developments and our techniques have been advancing rapidly over the years.

Proposed Payments for 1969-70 Grain Crop It is only when the produce leaves the farm that we step back almost a century and employ archaic and outmoded methods and equipment.
Looking back, I find it rather strange that 25 years ago we used to haul grain from the farm on which I was born by means of a 60-bushel grain-box drawn by two horses. All the machinery we used was horse-drawn. Today, although we have modern machinery and modern methods of transporting our grain, we still deliver the grain to the elevator to which we delivered 25 years ago. The distributing and handling techniques have not changed one iota over the years. If we wish to streamline and upgrade the efficiency of our grain handling techniques, I suggest that we begin by examining distribution and handling techniques at elevators. Costs could be cut there. When one analyses our present system of handling and distributing one will see that it is absurd

almost as absurd as attempting to instal a computor in a Model T Ford chassis.
There are conflicting views about measures such as acreage payments, and hardly a day goes by without someone giving his views or advice on this subject. One thing can be said about acreage payments in relation to cash advances on farm-stored grain: acreage payments would not lock a farmer into a pattern where all the cash he receives trickles away immediately to pay for inputs, which can only result in perpetuating and expanding the conditions that first caused the trouble. Acreage payments can be made very flexible from season to season or year to year. They could also provide the necessary freedom for a farmer to switch from one crop to another, to reduce his output of a product in slow demand in favour of another in short supply or to enable him to get out of farm production altogether.
As some hon. members have pointed out, we have assisted other great industries of this country-the automobile industry, the oil industry and the mining industry. Therefore, for the life of me I cannot see why we should not bail out an industry that is so vital not only to western Canada but to Canada as a whole. Because of the slowdown in the farm sector, combine manufacturers in Canada have laid off employees. The result has been that the economy of western Canada has lagged. I am suggesting that this government should try to cure the problem and not merely prolong its life.

For one reason or another the western grain producer has been encouraged over the years to concentrate on the production of grain. He has been told to expand his grain acreage so that we can feed the hungry peoples of the world. Now conditions in the world have changed and world markets have demonstrated inadequacies of our system of distribution and marketing. At present we have huge amounts of unsold grain. Although the hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that one should not look only at percentages when considering world markets, I submit he should have listened to the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who said we are not penetrating existing markets and obtaining our fair percentage of existing international markets.
The western farmer, in short, has been told that he has acted incorrectly. He is blamed for his present troubles and is told by the government and various experts that he should stop farming grain and produce something else. Everyone knows how much it costs a manufacturer to re-tool when he wishes to produce a new model, let alone diversify and manufacture a new product. How is the western farm to re-tool, so to speak, and produce beef instead of grain, or go into dairy farming, when he has neither the expertise nor the capital to do so? Why is the farmer not receiving the advice and assistance of the Department of Agriculture in this regard? Has the department suffered because of the government's austerity program? Perhaps the entire department will be written off in the austerity drive and the staffs of the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State will be built up.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

After I have finished, ii the hon. member does not mind. If the government is serious about stimulating agricultural production, let us see some evidence of plans to provide long-term assistance and guidance, because to allow things to drift along from one inadequate emergency measure to another is simply to doom Canadian agriculture to gradual extinction. If this is the government's intention, let it be honest enough to admit it; It could then perhaps justify to the Canadian public this fundamental economic upheaval. Let us pass this measure by all means, Mr. Chairman, but let us at the same time resolve to build a practical and meaningful agricultural policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the House is fully aware that western agriculture, in particular, faces a major crisis. We have taken the most unusual step in this debate today of proceeding on all stages of the bill with a minimum of discussion. We have done this because, all hon. members realize that although the present bill is just another palliative to deal with this major crisis, it will nevertheless provide some temporary relief, particularly to those areas of western Canada which have not been able to harvest their grain.

This afternoon I want to get from the Minister without Portfolio responsible to the government for these matters a response to a proposal that has come from the farmers themselves. It has been pressed for over six months, and unfortunately up to this moment there has been no positive reply from the government or from the minister concerned. I think in the history of Canada's grain producers they have demonstrated their capacity to adjust to the extreme conditions and fluctuations of the grain industry.
Only a few years ago the government was urging the farmers to grow more and more grain. They were told that if they grew the grain, it could be sold. The prairie farmers responded in a magnificent way. We know this only too well because of the amazing production figures of the past four or five years. Productivity, stream-lined, improved techniques, technological changes and all the other measures adopted brought an almost immediate response to the request of the government for greater grain sales. There is obviously still some of this thinking in government circles. I have in my hand a Canadian Press release from Stratford, Ontario, which states as follows:
Arthur Laing, federal Minister of Public Works, said here Wednesday that Canada's wheat surpluses will be eaten up if the world population explosion continues.

I hope the Minister without Portfolio includes the Minister of Public Works in his group because there seems to be a lack of consensus within the cabinet as to the nature of the problem. This news release, incidentally, was publicized quite generally across Canada. It only adds to the confusion which already exists in the minds of farmers because of the lack of specific information and lack of consensus as to the true nature of the problem.
I would once again like to draw to the minister's attention the proposal of the prairie grain farmers with respect to the basic problem, the sale of grain. They can produce the best quality grain in the world. It is up to the Canadian government, through the Wheat Board, to ensure that the markets are maintained. Notwithstanding the Prime Minister's statement in this regard a little over a year ago in Winnipeg, it is still the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board to sell the grain.
According to the Minister of Public Works, the population explosion ensures that the market is still there. I am sure the minister is aware of this proposal; a paper on the subject is before him. It is a positive one. It does not involve any additional expenditure on the part of the government; it merely suggests that a Canadian export marketing organization for Canadian grain be established. It would involve organizing a Canadian-owned company charged with the responsibility of selling Canadian-produced grains. The agency would not be financed from public funds; it would be financed through deducting up to one per cent per bushel on all grain delivered to the Canadian Wheat Board at the various elevator points. It is envisaged that this agency would be licensed by the Canadian Wheat Board as a marketing agency for Canadian grains.
The purpose of the corporation would be to sell grains produced in Canada and to develop new markets for products which can be produced by western Canadian farmers in obvious abundance. When such an agency had been established, it is conceivable that it could make arrangements with other agricultural commodity groups to develop export markets for their products as well. Marketing is the greatest problem of Canadian agriculture at the moment. If we could market the agricultural products, the current difficulties which are being handled by the nostrums and palliatives such as the one before us would be completely unnecessary.

It should be noted that this proposed agency would in no way compete with the function of the Canadian Wheat Board or the present Canadian grain trade, but would supplement their efforts by having salesmen strategically located throughout the world to continually assess the trading activities and market requirements, and to promote the sale of Canadian products on these markets. This is an excellent example of the sort of selfhelp philosophy that has made it possible for the prairie grain farmer to survive with the almost impossible changes and challenges of the grain industry.
Some preliminary government assistance would be necessary. This would be of a very minimal nature. It is envisaged that in order to get this agency organized and operating successfully it would be necessary to have the assistance of the federal government in the following ways. At first, there would have to be initial financing for the first year of operations, that is, before the collections could be made from the farmers. No doubt any outlay on the part of the treasury would be repaid on the basis of the farmers' contribution.
Second, the federal government would participate or take the initiative in establishing a research and development arm to continually assess market developments and encourage a production program to fill those markets. This could be the function of the Canada Grains Council; it could be assigned this responsibility. Third, export credit assistance on reasonable terms to countries requiring this type of credit could be made available by the federal government.
In passing I would like to note that one of the reasons, if not the main reason, for the successful sales to China in the early 1960s was based precisely on this point. The federal government of the day made reasonable credit terms available to the Chinese government. It did this on the basis of face-to-face negotiations between politicians at the ministerial level.
The fourth point is this. Assistance by the various trade commissioners stationed throughout the world, in contacting buyers and helping with communications and import regulations, could be made available to the qualified salesmen who would be the essential aspect of the export corporation. Fifth, the support of the Canadian Wheat Board and the federal government would be necessary to allow for flexible pricing and trading

arrangements in order to successfully conclude the sales. This proposal has been put forward by the farmers as a result of a series of meetings organized at what we call the grass roots level and has been in the hands of the federal government for almost six months. We sometimes talk about unfair competition from other grain exporting countries, particularly France and the United States. I would point out that the United States has already taken action to stimulate exports through increased sales. They have organized an export marketing service which comes directly under the United States Department of Agriculture. One task of this new service is to maximize the export of agricultural products. I understand that this United States agency will be backed by farm programs calculated to maintain prices at realistic levels which will allow commodities to move into world markets. We can be certain that the United States will be embarking upon aggressive efforts to market grain and other products around the world, and that Canada's experience in recent years with respect to United States' competition will be even worse unless we gird our loins and accept the good, practical recommendations which have come from the farmers themselves.
I do not think it is necessary to discuss this particular recommendation any further, but I would appreciate it if the minister would comment on this excellent proposal before the debate closes. What is even more important, I trust he will announce that action is to be taken on this matter before Christmas. Certainly, Parliament has demonstrated its willingness to act with the greatest possible speed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: NATO-REPORT BY SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ON BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you I have no objection to having two separate rounds. I thought my suggestion might suit the convenience of the opposition. That was the only reason I put it forward.
There is a coming together of events in Europe today that opens the way to profound change. Basic differences between East and West will not be resolved overnight but there is reason to believe that a new era of genuine negotiation has begun.
Three new developments herald this era of change. The most important, which may well turn out to be a turning point in post-war history, is the opening in Helsinki last month of preliminary discussions between the United States and the Soviet Union on the limitation of strategic nuclear weapons, the so-called SALT talks. The ground for these talks was prepared in NATO, and at last week's meeting Secretary of State Rogers gave us a confidential report on progress to date. The very fact that these talks have begun in a businesslike way has changed the East-West climate and brought a sense of cautious hope into East-West relations.
The second development of major importance is the manifest intention of West Germany to work out new relationships with East Germany, Poland, the Soviet Union and other countries of Eastern Europe. This new West German policy has added new momentum to the search for negotiated settlements in Europe.
The third development of potentially historic significance was last week's summit meeting of the six Common Market countries at the Hague. The extent of agreement achieved at this meeting has created a new mood of optimism and co-operation in Western Europe, a development which will encourage new approaches to the problems of Europe as a whole.
It was in this atmosphere of movement and progress that the NATO ministers discussed and defined their common position. They did so in the knowledge that the outcome of their meeting as made known to both East and West by the communique and declaration, and by less formal but still important press
December 8, 1969

Report on Brussels Meeting reports, would become part of the evolving discourse among the nations roncerned with the future Europe and its people.
The NATO Council functions not only as an important point of exchange and consultation for the ideas and intentions of its members, but also as a transmitting station for signals to the other side. The issues before the recent meeting were, simply stated, what ideas and intentions should be conveyed to the countries of Eastern Europe, and in what ways they should be carried forward. All those present at the meeting had very much in mind that the ideas conveyed and the manner of their communication should be such as to make clear our desire to improve relations and negotiate outstanding issues. For our own part, in our contribution to the Brussels meeting we sought to advocate attitudes and measures which would be both realistic and conciliatory, to steer between the rigid no and the unthinking yes.
At the meeting I put forward the view that NATO should seize the initiative by showing a clear willingness to start discussion of specific issues. The inclusion in the declaration of a proposal for early discussions on mutual and balanced force reductions in Europe is one example of this, in the sensitive but vital field of arms control. This proposal is an advance on the previous NATO' position and one that we actively promoted. We would have preferred a more precise formula, making clear, for instance, the regional limits and other detailed conditions which in the view of NATO members would govern any such force reductions. Others felt that such specifics should await some response from the nations of Eastern Europe, which up to now has not been forthcoming.
The declaration contains a section on Germany and Berlin which, among other things, gives support to the proposals of the West German government for a modus vivendi between the two parts of Germany and for a related bilateral exchange of declarations on the non-use of force. I have no doubt of the firm resolve of Chancellor Willy Brandt's government to break new ground in searching for solutions to the complex problems which have divided Europe for a generation. The response of the East to these overtures will be an important test of their intentions. The news this morning that negotiations have begun between the Soviet Union and the Federal German Republic on an exchange of declarations renouncing the use of force is a hopeful sign.

[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I also suggested that it would be useful to broaden the East-West dialogue to include discussion of non-political subjects such as the pollution of the environment, about which both sides are increasingly concerned, and the declaration also invites co-operation on this topic.
There has been much public discussion of the idea of a European security conference. I hope that such a conference will be held, at the right time and in the right circumstances. Such a conference is only one way of making progress toward the settlement of European problems, and for the time being it may not be the most effective.
Bilateral governmental contacts between countries of Eastern and Western Europe are a commonplace today, and there are many multilateral opportunities that underline the point that there is no shortage of meeting places or meetings. Canada attaches great importance to this process and plays an active part as illustrated by the recent visit to Ottawa of the Soviet Foreign Minister, Mr. Gromyko.
Second, I do not doubt that if and when it appears that a full security conference would be productive of tangible results, it could be readily organized. I am equally certain that Canada would be among the participating nations. What does, however, concern many western governments is that if such a conference were held prematurely it might prejudice the important progressive trends now so promising in Europe. Negotiations can make progress only when the other side displays a readiness to talk about something more than a mere freezing of the status quo in Europe. It would not make sense for the western countries to be beguiled into a conference where the cards are stacked in advance against an outcome reasonably acceptable to both sides. The consensus emerging from the meeting reflects these factors, while keeping open the door to a conference.
The problem of procedures for organizing negotiations with the other side is a complex one. Bilateral contacts may be more suitable at present for some issues, limited multilateral discussions for others, and a general conference including the neutral nations of Europe will probably become appropriate in due course. We proposed some weeks ago that there should now be a detailed Alliance study of this question of procedures for negotiation, and I am very pleased to report that, follow-
December 8, 1969

ing the Canadian suggestion, the declaration includes a specific request to have the NATO Council study this issue and report on it to our next ministerial meeting in May.
Discussions at NATO meetings are necessarily detailed and sometimes technical. It is not easy to get agreement when 15 governments, each with its own essential national interests and its own way of looking at things, are involved. I can tell the House, however, that some real progress was made last week. It was encouraging to me, and to all who were with me, to find a new and more hopeful atmosphere and a new resolve that the arid confrontation that has for too long characterized East-West relations should be brought to an end. Not by any sudden dramatic initiative, but by steady and careful negotiation of specific issues, starting with those that show the best chances for success.
We found a new climate in Europe, a new dynamic in the Common Market that points the way to enlargement of the Community and strengthening of ties between its members, a new German government already working toward modus vivendi with East Germany. Above all, we found a new atmosphere of hope brought about by the promise of progress in the SALT talks. I was encouraged, as I know all members of this House will be, to find NATO sensitive to the new trends, contributing to the great events that are taking place, and looking beyond its essential defence functions to the opportunities for a more positive role in securing the peace in Europe.
I took advantage of the NATO meetings to have individual talks with some of my NATO colleagues. I met with the foreign ministers of Italy and Turkey and had brief sessions with the German foreign minister and the United States Secretary of State. I also had a useful discussion with the French foreign minister of our bilateral relations and I am glad to say that there was mutual agreement that we should work out arrangements to avoid future incidents of the kind that have marred our relations in the recent past. I am hopeful that in this way we may be able to put our relations on a better footing.

Mr. Speaker, I would like at this time to report to hon. members on the meeting in Brussels last Wednesday of the NATO Defence Planning Committee and the NATO Nuclear Affairs Committee.
Members will recall that it is at the regular December ministerial meeting of the Defence Planning Committee that final undertakings are made on each nation's force contribution. Canada's contribution for 1970 is the reconstructed force for NATO Europe and the Supreme Allied Command Atlantic, announced in my statement of September 19 last.
In my remarks to the Defence Planning Committee I referred to the committee's meeting last May at which I announced Canada's intention to reduce the size of our military contribution to NATO. I then told the committee that this change was occasioned, in part, by a requirement for budgetary restraints on all Canadian government activities.
I reminded the meeting that, after full consultation, we had reached agreement on the final extent and timings of our proposed adjustment in Europe, and said that as a result of consultation we had modified considerably our original plan. These modifications were embodied in the force structure I announced on September 19.
The communique refers to the meaningful negotiations we carried out in paragraph 10, which reads in part:
Ministers took note of the positive outcome of consultations with the Canadian authorities concerning their forces for NATO, which were initiated following the Defence Planning meeting of 28th May, 1969.
I am happy to report that the European nations have initiated steps to adjust their forces to maintain the NATO force levels in Europe and, while their plans have not been finally completed, it appears that they will be shortly.

During the ministerial meeting, the 12 ministers comprising the Nuclear Defence Affairs Committee reviewed the work of the smaller seven-member Nuclear Planning
21545-36}

Report on Brussels Meeting Group and considered two papers which were originated by the Planning Group and which were adopted by the Defence Planning Committee.
These papers dealt with procedures for political consultation on the possible use of nuclear weapons and guidance for Commanders on drawing up their plans for the possible defensive tactical use of nuclear weapons in defence of the Treaty area.
Speaking for Canada, I supported the adoption of these papers which further define and restrict the circumstances under which nuclear weapons might be used, emphasizing the requirement for political consultation and control.
As honourable members may recall, the Nuclear Planning Group changes its membership on a rotation basis so that the nonnuclear members have an opportunity, together with the nuclear powers, to participate in the planning for nuclear defence measures, including control and consultation procedures. Canada was a member from January 1967 to July 1968 and will become a member again starting 1st January, 1970, for a period of 18 months.
In my further remarks, Mr. Speaker, I felt it appropriate to deal with Canada's contribution, past and present, to the NATO Alliance.
I reminded the Committee that twenty years ago Canada willingly helped to establish the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Like the other members, we pledged ourselves to consider an armed attack against one or more of us in Europe or in North America, as an attack against us all. We still hold that pledge.

I said that the long period of the NATO alliance had enabled European members to complete their post-war recovery and embark on a period of economic growth with peace and stability. Behind the NATO shield, western Europe has grown strong and prosperous. To be sure, the military threat has not diminished in Europe or in North America. I said that to help meet this threat, and to help build the NATO shield behind which western Europe could continue her post-war recovery, Canada alone gave over $1 billion in mutual aid in the first ten years of NATO. Every European NATO country has benefited from our mutual aid program.


Referring to other Canadian contributions, I said that during the first ten critical years of NATO Canada contributed over $413 million toward NATO aircrew training, and this has now risen to over $446 million. Our NATO military budget contributions total over $46 million, and our infrastructure contributions have amounted to over $181 million. All in all, our total Canadian defence contributions to the European NATO countries amount to well over $2 billion, and this figure does not include the cost of maintaining our forces in Europe.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that we are proud of our contributions and do not begrudge them; but I reminded the committee that, in addition to our contribution to NATO Europe, Canada also contributes heavily to the defence of North America, and particularly to the defence of the United States deterrent which protects us all.
I reminded the meeting that we have not decreased our defence budget but, like many NATO partners, we have had to absorb inflationary costs which have meant a reduction in manpower and an adjustment in our force levels.
I said that in our defence review we had to look at all of these facts which form a very complex equation. On the one hand, we have made substantial defence contributions of well over $2 billion to NATO Europe over and above the cost of stationing our forces there, while at the same time contributing to the defence of NATO North America. On the other hand, there is a growing belief in Canada that Europe is in a much better position now to absorb more of the costs than she was 10 or 15 years ago. At the same time we know that there is a continuing threat to NATO North America.
I said that one solution, as we see it, is to show our European partners that we do recognize the continuing threat to NATO Europe. It is for this reason that we will continue to maintain forces in Europe. But, I said, our European partners must recognize all of the factors I listed and accept the fact that there are two sides to the equation.
I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying this:
NATO is not Europe. NATO is not North America. NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization-a group of nations banded together which are pledged to consider an attack against one or more of us in Europe or North America as an attack against all of us. We reaffirm that pledge.

The Department of Transport has been involved in studies of the noise problem since 1960 when jet aircraft were first introduced on regular scheduled service.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe we have to begin by reminding ourselves that there was a change in strategy. Massive retaliation was the strategic concept employed before, and that was changed two years ago to the concept of flexible response. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
In the opinion of this House, the government by failing to establish a parliamentary committee to 
concern itself with the problems of urban people of Canada has neglected an important means of coming to grips with those problems and this House urges that such a committee be established forthwith.
He said: Mr. Speaker, not very far from this chamber in which we are meeting another meeting between the leaders of the governments of the ten provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and his associates is taking place. There, they are discussing the constitutional framework within which Canada will exist in the future. They are discussing the division of powers between the two levels of government. They are discussing the use of the spending power by the government of Canada. They are discussing the taxing powers; that is to say, the allocation of revenue sources between the federal and provincial governments. They are also discussing the question of regional disparities.
There is, as we all know, a third level of government in this country, a third level of government that governs the same Canadian citizens and admittedly the same Canadian taxpayers, but which governs them in a different way and under a different jurisdiction. In many respects, it is a level of government that is closer to the people.
We recognize generally, I think, that burdens on municipal governments today are extremely heavy. These governments bear onerous responsibilities to their people, responsibilities that are growing in weight, becoming even more complex and bearing very strong personal, human and social implications. They are also responsibilities that are growing in cost. One might say that they are growing in cost at an enormous rate, though the same can be said at all levels of government.
Municipalities are, of course, more limited than any other level of government so far as access to sources of revenue is concerned. Property tax and grants from the provincial treasuries pretty well make up the list of sources of revenue available to municipalities. They have difficulty in financing services and therefore, in some cases at least, there is a decline in the quality of municipal services. Certainly, there is a great deal of inequality and disparity from municipal government to municipal government in various parts of the country. Indeed, I think there is an acknowledged inadequacy of municipal services relative to the need in almost all cases. I have very serious concern as to whether our provincial governments have the financial resources to cope with this severe situation in
December 8. 1969

Urban Problems
association with the municipalities and within their jurisdiction. All these problems are germane to the present motion before the House. They are perhaps more relevant to a discussion which will probably take place later this week on the problems and prospects of Canadian cities. I understand two days are being set aside later in the week for the purpose of such a discussion.
Suffice it to say for now that municipalities are bystanders at the constitutional conference. They do not have a seat or a direct voice in respect of constitutional review. I am not assuming in presenting this motion that they ought to have such a seat or voice directly. Certainly, I am not saying in presenting this motion that we ought to attempt to re-divide constitutional powers or responsibilities among three levels of government rather than two. The chances are that things would be even more chaotic then than they are now. The problems and responsibilities of municipal governments will have to be brought more adequately into discussions of constitutional review. We will be dealing with this in more detail later on in the week, assuming that the Government provides the opportunity to do so by setting aside the two days that have been discussed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
We will have an opportunity before too long, as I understand the intention of the Government, to take part in such a debate. In any event, I want to emphasize today that municipal governments are not only left out of effective participation in the process of long term constitutional review- that is the process of determining the future shape of our country-but as well, with pressing problems facing the people who live in our cities, the municipalities are not receiving the attention of Parliament or the attention of the Government of Canada. That is the reason for this motion.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) tried some days ago to obtain the unanimous consent of the House to move for the establishment of a committee to provide the type of forum suggested today. He was denied consent by some of the urban members on the Liberal benches. I am glad to see quite a number of Government members
from our cities here today, Toronto for example. I thought we might have to send our whip out to get them. At Harrison Hot Springs there took place what some people thought was a confrontation between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and some of the urban members of his own party. Actually, Sir, it was just sort of a love spat.
May I say it is implicit in the proposal that is put before the House today that a parliamentary committee should be established. Implicit in this, is our belief that Parliament as an institution, and members of parliament as individuals, have a positive contribution to make in the development of an effective urban policy for Canada. A refusal by the Government must be regarded as one more attempt by the Prime Minister and his cabinet to limit the role of Parliament and the role of parliamentarians. A refusal to accept this motion would cast more light on this Government's attitude toward participatory democracy and on its reasons for urging what it calls parliamentary reform.
I have expressed my view and my fears before that reforms imposed by closure on Parliament last summer indicated a desire to make Parliament more subservient to the Government. If I correctly read the transcript of the television interview, yesterday, I think, by the independent member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) that fear was also shared by some members of the Government caucus at that time. The hon. member for Spadina indicated that, at the same time the Government was tightening controls on Parliament it was also tightening controls' on its own caucus.
The official word was that the committee system of Parliament would be reformed to allow private members a more active role. Anyone familiar with the workings of this House, however, knows that although members might be busier in committee now they are certainly not more influential. The government retains the power even to change the reports of committees. It clearly retains the power to impose a party line upon Government members of a parliamentary committee.
It is early yet to call that reform a sham, but it is time to say that the Government attitude toward the committees of Parliament has not revealed a willingness to give any real freedom or really important function to private members of Parliament. If the Government refuses now to establish even a committee concerned with urban affairs, it will confirm I suggest its contempt for the private members

of its own party and of Parliament. It will indicate that in the view of the Government it is not only the members of the Opposition who are nobodies.
In that connection, and because it is important to the principle of giving private members and Parliament a useful role in meeting the urban challenge in Canada, I want to quote very briefly from an article by Mr. Gordon Pape in the November 26 issue of the Montreal Gazette. He had quoted earlier in the article statements by Mr. Marc Lalonde, the principal secretary to the Prime Minister. Mr. Lalonde was talking about the conference at Harrison Hot Springs and the suspicion with which the Government would regard any recommendations which differed from its own policy. Mr. Pape wrote:
What he appeared to be telling the other members of his discussion group was that only the Government is in a position to formulate valid policy because only it has access to all the relevant information required to do so. If the party decides on some other course, it is not because the Government is wrong, but only because the policy it has chosen has not been explained fully enough.
The inescapable conclusion, if this is really what he meant, is that the only realistic role of party members is to follow the course chosen by their leaders since the chiefs are the only ones in possession of enough facts to make meaningful decisions.
Earlier Mr. Lalonde had said that if a Liberal policy conference disagreed with the Government and, therefore, by his logic indicated that the policy conference was wrong, then the cabinet ministers would have to get out and do a selling job. It is thus established that the East Block views members of cabinet as salesmen. It is interesting to speculate what views the East Block may hold toward mere members of Parliament.
Perhaps they would let them do a little selling as well. Perhaps in the view of the East Block the role of urban members of Parliament is to tell the people what the Government is doing for them. Therefore the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) can go back and tell the people of Winnipeg that Ottawa is making them, in the words of Mayor Juba, the largest Indian reservation in Canada, without the benefit of adequate federal help to meet the cost of welfare and unemployment. The hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Loiselle) can then go back to Montreal and say, "Look at all the lovely unemployment". The members from downtown Toronto can go home and tell their constituents how effectively the Government is applying immigration laws to keep their

families out. That is the role of the urban member in the just society.

Indeed, that sounds suspiciously like the plea that brought many of the government members into Parliament in the first place. We hope we will hear from them this afternoon and this evening. We also hope that they will match their words with action by supporting the proposal for a parliamentary committee. I want to assure them that we do not hold so harsh a view of them as do some of their "betters" in cabinet.
I am sure hon. members opposite were interested to read the column of that well known political commentator, Douglas Fisher, in the Telegram of December 5. Mr. Fisher was discussing the resignation from the government caucus of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan). He wrote:
One minister told me: "It's always the quiet ones who make the clean moves. We've been listening to Givens and Otto complain and grandstand for several years. They want the reputation of being independent. But it was the guy who never hectored or played his wrongs to the media who bolted. A lot of us feel badly over that; however, it won't make us an easier mark for the belly-achers."
If there are any bellyachers over there, I leave it to them to decide which diplomat in the cabinet offered that judgment. Perhaps they might take the opportunity today to indicate to their constituents just where they stand on questions of a role for Parliament in urban affairs. I give you my personal assurance that this is one vote your constituents will hear about.

We can say this for the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens). Of the two inanimate objects which he helped to bring to Nathan Phillips Square, the Archer has been more useful to Toronto than the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to date, and in the end it will probably prove even more popular.
Many parts of Canada have been disappointed by this government. But the dejection and defection in the cities is particularly critical, precisely because it affects so many young Canadians and so many of the active and talented people whose energies and dedication the nation needs.
It is to the credit of the Prime Minister's election campaign that he inspired among this critical minority an excitement about Canada. If his campaign turned them on, however, his performance is turning them off, and turning them away. It is making cynics of the people upon whose dynamic optimism the country depends.
The Prime Minister makes much of a claim that he promised next to nothing during that election campaign. That is presumably his excuse for doing next to nothing in office. But the fact is clear that, whatever was said, the Liberal party consciously campaigned on the promise that it would form a modern government, oriented to the young, to the future and to the cities. When the Prime Minister said "come, follow me", Canadians assumed he meant to go somewhere, he meant to take them forward, not that he was going to ask them to go backwards with him. This government has demonstrated no more interest in the cities than it has in the poor. It treats them as problems to shift to other jurisdictions, rather than problems to solve or challenges to meet.
This motion should have the support of all members of the House. Certainly, it is inconceivable that any member from a large city riding could possibly vote against it. In a moderate and constructive way, this motion represents one step to halt the growing alienation of city dwellers. There is a crisis of confidence in the cities. People are quickly losing confidence not just in the present government, although that is certainly true, but in the capacity of governmental institutions generally to cope effectively with their problems. There is disillusionment and frustration in the cities. It is very serious, and must be taken seriously by Parliament.
It is my strong conviction that the government is not using the potential of the present constitution for a federal role in the cities in
Urban Problems
connection with urban problems, admittedly as a partner, but as a working partner. The municipal structures of government are unquestionably the constitutional responsibility of the provinces. So are generally all things of a merely local or private nature in the province. But to argue, as the Prime Minister seems to, that the federal government is constitutionally crippled when it comes to cities and their people, is illogical in my view.
The federal government, under our constitution, has a great many powers related to urban matters. Its role in housing and urban renewal is not seriously challenged. It is also responsible, for example, for major decisions concerning airports and their services, and all forms of rail transportation, which surely provides a legitimate basis for an active role in urban transit problems in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities involved. The federal government is responsible for its own great variety of federal buildings, facilities and installations, and for all those of the Crown agencies which can put it in the middle of major urban planning. Federal jurisdiction over communications in the widest sense, from that of land wire and microwave systems to the postal authority, offers opportunity for a more active, instead of a passive, federal presence in the cities.
My disposition is to use the latitude of the present constitution and find ways for the federal government to be useful to the people who live in our cities. In my view, a parliamentary committee on urban problems could be concerned with the federal role in helping to solve problems, always in co-operation with the other two levels of government.
Three main responsibilities occur to me for such a committee as I am proposing: first, to provide a national forum and a national focus for the discussion of urban problems and their consideration. Second, the committee could hear directly from municipal governments and provincial authorities in a public way on how the federal involvement in our cities can be made more effective on a continuing basis. Third, the committee could discuss and make periodic recommendations to Parliament and to the government on specific problems and opportunities for federal action or assistance.
I could have added a fourth role for this committee, to the effect that the committee could also provide an opportunity for some of the members of Parliament on the government side of the House to make the kind of representations about urban problems that

they are unable to make now except perhaps privately.
