It is fitting that this debate should occur on the very day that another round of constitutional discussions begins. The fact that the problem of the constitution and the problem of the federal role in the cities are being discussed in different places on the same day indicates that, to a large degree, they are separate questions-not entirely, but to a large degree. Of course, there are constitutional implications. There are constitutional implications to virtually everything in a federal state, if you insist on getting hung-up on them. In the case of a federal role in the cities, many of the constitutional implications are substantial. But the fact remains that the government and the Parliament of Canada can do much more to help out in the cities, to help with urban problems, without changing a comma in the existing constitution of Canada.
It is recognized that the Prime Minister has a mental block about the constitution, and has imposed his view on the government. But what is at issue here is not so much a concept of federalism as a concept of active government compared to passive government. The federal government has the power. It is already active in the cities, causing problems if not solving them. Our desire today is simply to acknowledge that role and that obligation, to establish some machinery which will symbolize the concern of Parliament with urban Canada and urban problems, and allow this body to work systematically on the proper exercise of the existing federal power in connection with urban affairs.
I challenge hon. members from urban areas to vote for this motion, to state clearly and unequivocally that as a first step we want this committee to be set up and to get to work- yes, get to work, Sir-to bridge the gap between the urban citizens of Canada and their national institutions. So, Sir, I move the motion that you have put to the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic Party would like to commend the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for bringing this motion to the attention of the House at this time, urging the necessity of setting up a parliamentary committee to concern itself with the problems of urban people. Not only do we support this motion, but we would move one step further by recommending the 
establishment of a separate ministry of housing and urban affairs, with a full-time minister, so that once a committee does reach conclusions or recommendations on these problems we would have a full-time minister to implement them.
The Leader of the Opposition has given two reasons why he brought this motion to the House at this time. I would suggest a third reason. The recent United States presidential commission report on crime and violence has sparked and prodded many members to take a good look at what is happening here in Canada. That commission made two important findings. The first is that violent crime in the United States is primarily a phenomenon of the cities. This is a fact of central importance. The New York Times recently published excerpts from the commission's report, and from it I quote:
Large cities have the highest reported violent crime levels per unit of population. Smaller cities, suburbs and rural areas have lower levels. The average rate of major violent offences in cities of over 250,000 inhabitants is 11 times greater than in rural areas, eight times greater than in suburban areas, and five and one-half times greater than in cities with 50,000 to 100,000 inhabitants.
The second important finding of the commission was that violent crime in the city is concentrated especially among youths between the ages of 15 and 20 years. Again I quote:
Urban arrest rates for homicide are much higher among the 18-24 age group than among any other; for rape, robbery and aggravated assault, arrests in the 15-24 age group far outstrip those of any other group. Moreover, it is in these age groups that the greatest increases in all arrest rates have occurred. Surprisingly, however, there have also been dramatic and disturbing increases in arrest rates of the 10-14 age group for two categories-a 300 per cent increase in assault between 1958 and 1967, and 200 per cent in robbery in the same period.
This indicates the extreme urgency and importance of this matter at this time.
Not only did the U.S. commission present recommendations and findings but it also projected what might happen if immediate remedial action is not taken. For instance, it states that central business districts in the hearts of cities will be frequented by business people and shoppers during the day time, and thus will be afforded protection by these people, but in the evening they will be deserted except for police patrols. This report also indicates that high rise apartment buildings will become fortified cells protected by private guards and security devices; that suburban areas will be protected only by their
December 8, 1969

distance from densely populated areas, and that the ownership of guns will become almost universal. Central residential neighbourhoods and streets will be unsafe in differing degrees with ghetto slum neighbourhoods becoming places of terror, entirely out of police control in the evenings. Armed guards will be protecting schools, libraries and playgrounds, and there will be an intensification of group hatred, more violence, and the defensive response will become more elaborate.
These were the findings of the U.S. commission on crime and violence, and this bad dream could become a reality in Canada. This fact has worried many Canadians, especially in light of the recent riots in Montreal. Everytime I hear the words "commission" or "task force" I am reminded of the quip of a U.S. congressman who said that a short time ago when Americans were confronted with a problem they usually threw money at it and hoped it would go away. But later they developed a more sophisticated response and set up commissions and task forces to meet problems. We have the same experience in Canada. I can think of the task force on housing, the commission on drugs, the Senate commission on poverty, the veterans affairs study, the recent studies on corrections and juvenile delinquency and the recent and important study on labour. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have set up many commissions and task forces, but have taken very little action with regard to the problems.
One of the main reasons for the lack of action is the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), something referred to by the Leader of the Opposition. It seems that the Prime Minister is claustrophobically ensconced in a constitutional straitjacket and is not willing to move on some of these major problems. If we were to implement some of the recommendations that have been made by commissions and task forces in Canada we would be taking a big step towards alleviating the problems of the urban dwellers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the problems of urban people in Canada? Briefly stated they are poverty, unemployment, a housing crisis, drugs, alienation of youth, and the changing role of the family. It has become a cliche to say that we live in a rapidly changing society, yet this has never been more true than it is today. In 1980, 80 per cent of all Canadians will live in urban centres, compared with 70 per cent in 1961, and Canada will be made up of urban families with an urban style of life.
21545-37J
Urban Problems
The average family, Mr. Speaker, will decrease in size from three or four to one or two, reversing the tendency of the last 40 years. Both married and single women will participate more actively in the labour force. Women will be better educated and many married women will work throughout their married lives, withdrawing only for brief periods of motherhood activities. The mother's income has become, and will continue to be, essential to provide the goods and services available.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Canadians are being forced out of their single family detached dwellings into high-rise apartments, thereby becoming cliff dwellers. Young people are maturing earlier, both physically and in social sophistication. Many are remaining longer in universities and technical schools in order to equip themselves for the technological labour force. Fathers are losing the traditional role of breadwinner and "pater familias" and the mother's income has become an integral part of the family income. This is changing the family picture and very little can be done about it; however, there are other areas in which much can be done.
The first problem is that of poverty. Canadians are perplexed by the continuing spectre of the poverty level income on which 30 per cent of the population lives.
In a recent study by Mrs. J. R. Podoluk entitled "Incomes of Canadians", she stated:
The 1961 census shows that some 916,000 nonfarm families and 416,000 individuals-a total of about 4,200,000 people, including 1,700,000 children under 16 years of age-are in the low-income group. In addition, the number of farm families in the low-income group is estimated to be 150,000 consisting of possibly 550,000 persons, or more than half of the estimated 275,000 families primarily dependent on farming for a livelihood. The total estimated low-income group is thus just under 29 per cent of the population. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics identifies low income as less than $1,500 for one, $2,500 for two, $3,000 for three, $3,500 for four and $4,000 for five or more in 1961 dollars.
These amounts are based chiefly on the criterion that any individual is in the low-income group if he has to spend 70 per cent or more of his income on the necessities of life, i.e. food, clothing, shelter.
A quick accounting would indicate that 4.8 million people in Canada live below the poverty line. In other words, poverty is a harsh reality in our country today and it is no longer measured in statistical terms. If poverty is measured in the classical sense of people literally starving to death, unable to sustain life, then poverty is eliminated in Canada

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
because it would only involve 1 or 2 per cent of the population. If it is measured as a condition in which families or individuals are entirely dependent upon welfare for food, clothing and shelter, then it has been reduced to minimum proportions. But if we measure poverty as a denial to some individuals and families of a reasonable share of what science, technology and the general economy has made available, that is education, good health, privacy and leisure activities-the style portrayed in television and the glamour magazines-then 80 per cent of Canadians are impoverished.
We have to look at poverty in a new sense and with a new definition, Mr. Speaker. As has been stated, a person is poverty stricken when he has a deep sense of inequality and feels an economic exclusion and alienation from the wider society in which he lives. Surely, that must apply to many groups in Canadian life today, more especially our youth-the single parent families, the blind and disabled, the retarded, the senior citizen, the unemployed and the homeless people.
What can we do about them, Mr. Speaker? I should not say what can we do, but what must we do? First of all, we must maintain and create a high rate of economic growth with a high rate of employment. I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is listening to this, because it is very important. Employment is the key to the poverty problem. When a person has a sense of achievement, a sense of dignity, a sense of pride and respect, these go a long way toward establishing a full and secure life. People had some of these values in wartime when there was full employment. Since the war, unemployment has increased and it is necessary that we strike at it and strike hard.
When I think of how the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and other cabinet ministers are attacking the problem of inflation, by increasing unemployment, I am not given much encouragement nor, I am sure, is the Minister of Labour. No person should be in a disadvantageous position simply because of his place of birth, province of residence or change of location. I am sure the Minister of Labour will agree with this.
The second approach to the problem of urban people, Mr. Speaker, should be a well-defined policy of housing and urban planning. In the recent report of the task force on housing, the following statement appears:
Here, too, Is poverty in its rawest and ugliest form. No pretty garden or painted cottages here to camouflage economic depression. Poverty in the
[Mr. Gilbert.)
worst areas of the city core is abundantly visible in the decrepit structures which form its housing, the cracked pavement of the streets which are its recreational area, and the rodents which are its wild life. This poverty you can see and hear and taste and smell. Its residents are not simply families struggling to catch up to the average national income; too often they are people fighting to retain a vestige of human dignity and selfrespect. No task force impression is more vivid of mind or depressing of spirit than those formed amid the blight and slum of Canada's larger cities.
Reading that, and remembering the fanfare when the task force presented its report as well as the whambang cross-country campaign, one wonders what happened to the recommendations of that task force. In fact, more than half the recommendations were on mortgage financing which would draw monies on housing to the upper-middle and upper classes, increasing the limit on mortgages to $35,000. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the report is a rejection of the pleas for additional funds for low-income housing, for public housing and urban renewal. Public housing became the whipping boy of the minister of the day. Now, we are most anxiously waiting for guidelines with regard to public housing and urban renewal.
It appears as though we are having trouble reaching the target of 200,000 homes in 1969. We in the New Democratic Party say there should be 250,000 to catch the shortfall of previous years; there should be land banks and direct loans to municipalities with low interest rates. The other day when I heard the Minister of Finance say that interest rates are "too damn high", the thought occurred to me that of course he is the man to correct them. But the minister just sits lazily by thinking that the market mechanism will reduce the interest rate.

be added to the scheme. May I at this time move an amendment to the motion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
'and this House also urges that the Government give consideration to the establishing of a Department of Housing and Urban Affairs and the appointment of a full-time Minister thereof.'.

I regard the intervention of the hon. gentleman as a compliment, and this applies to the shouting from the benches of his hon. friends. I have always found that when we are getting close to the bone the hon. member gets up and begins to complain. If the hon. member for Temiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) cannot win by reason-and I suppose that has never happened in the House-he tries to shout us down.
I have referred to the attitude of the provincial government of Ontario, for which, apparently, the Leader of the Opposition has such contempt. I refer, now, to another statement on the position, this time from the Premier of Quebec in the National Assembly on June 5. I quote a translation of it:
The conclusion to be drawn from this is that neither under the present constitution nor under the new constitution which is being negotiated at this time should there be any suggestion of handing over to the federal government any responsibility whatever in respect of municipalities. It is not because of the considerable importance which now attaches to urban problems that we should look to the federal government for their solutions.
December 8, 1969

Urban Problems
The most serious consequences of any federal intervention in this field would be, I feel, the introduction of an element of confusion where no such confusion now exists. Division of responsibilities between the two levels of government- the federal government on the one hand and provincial governments on the other-is difficult enough to determine as it is. Such being the case,
I fail to see why any attempt should be made to confuse the issue further by allowing the federal government to trespass in an area which is none of its concern.
Well, that is the attitude of the Premier of Quebec. I have already referred to the attitude of the Premier of Ontario who, nominally at least, is a supporter of the Leader of the Opposition. These views are an additional reason for using great caution before following the course proposed by the Leader of the Opposition; they are an argument for declining to make any substantial change in the arrangements which already exist for committees of the House. The opportunities are there, now, if the Official Opposition wishes to use them. Why should we play around with names, which, in effect, is what the motion proposes, at the risk of involving ourselves in a further constitutional crisis?
Let me say at once I entirely support the suggestion that we ought to show great concern for the problems now being faced by our cities. I am concerned by the fact that in Ontario we do not have any logical and well-planned provincial program for housing and the development of the province in the next 25 years. We, in Ontario, are deeply concerned about this but we are directing our representations to Queen's Park about it.
Unfortunately, hon. members opposite cannot afford to look to Queen's Park to remedy these defaults. Attitudes there, on the provincial level, have proved it to be impossible for municipal levels of government to obtain revenues from taxation sufficient to deal adequately with urban problems. For example, the Provincial Assessment Act, the very stuff and substance, the basis upon which the municipalities must carry on, is the responsibility of the province. What is being done by the province to share the burden more equitably? The Provincial Planning Act which, again, is the responsibility of the province, has been lying in disuse, or else it has not been modified so the authorities may plan effectively land use in the province.
If this motion can be regarded as being anything, it is an indirect expression by the Leader of the Opposition of no confidence in the manner in which the provinces-and he 21545-38
was once a leader of one of them-have carried on their business. In particular, because he spoke particularly in the context of Toronto and Ontario, he was criticizing specifically the leader of that province.
One suggestion he made, and one can readily believe it was founded on his ignorance of the situation, was that this government and this Parliament have done nothing about urban affairs. Let me remind him that this House passed last session a bill which hon. gentlemen opposite were pleased to support making changes in the National Housing Act having to do with urban renewal and public housing. Let me remind hon. members that more than 90 per cent of the capital cost of housing and urban renewal projects in Ontario, particularly in my own constituency of Toronto, has derived from this Act. Let me remind the House of the grants made by the federal government, such as the grant to the community improvement association in connection with Regent Park to deal with the social problems arising from public housing. Let me also remind the House of the extensive grants in connection with urban renewal, particularly in our cities, to enable plans to be prepared for future growth. I think it was generally acknowledged at the meeting my colleague the Minister without Portfolio and I attended, that it was at the lower levels of government that the failure had occurred.

Mr. Speaker, time is passing so I will carry on. It does not matter how the minister slices the cake, it is still his problem. I suggest the reasoning behind his arguments this afternoon will not weigh very heavily on the minds of the Canadian people, though they will realize that his attitude was one of arrogance, that his arguments were childish and lacked a sense of maturity.
If I were wrong in trying not to spread myself too thinly within the committee structure, then I say the government, too,, is wrong and equally as vulnerable as I at the next election. This government has continually shown its reluctance to admit it has a role to play in finding solutions to the mounting problems of urban growth. As a result, one can say it is suffering from a new political disease, that of urban impotence, a disease that has not afflicted the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
The diagnosis was almost complete when the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) made the headlines during the Hot Springs "love-in" with his classic confrontation with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding urban affairs.

speechtext:
That is a good point. I should like to know where all the urban members are so they can chastise us. I hope
December 8, 1969

Urban Problems
those who raise their hands will take part in this debate, rather than go to the press to record their thoughts. The hon. member for York West did his party a great service when he stood up to be counted. The hon. member was also projecting public opinion in his remarks. He placed emphasis on the jurisdictional problems among cities, the provinces and Ottawa. Without question, the diagnosis is now a conclusive one, as revealed through the resignation of the hon. member for Spadi-na (Mr. Ryan), who now joins the ranks of the farmer, the fisherman, the urban dweller, the Indian and a former cabinet minister, all of whom have expressed their disillusionment with the just society party.
The interesting question that can now be posed is: How many more members on the other side of the House, like the courageous member from Spadina, will stand up and be counted? I am sure the patience of many more is being tried. I feel that that is a statement that can be made. Indeed, I suggest that the Toronto area is loaded with such members and, as I said before, I hope they take part in this debate to register their criticism of the inertia of this government when it comes to solving the problems of the urban areas.
My leader has indicated that the hon. member for Spadina and others are welcome in our party if they can meet the necessary qualifications. I suggest one qualification is that they take a simple oath, and that this oath be as follows: "I, so and so, member for so and so, do hereby accept and believe in the proposition that Trudeaumania is kaput". That is all they have to do to be happily welcomed.
The government's exchange of diplomats with the Vatican is one thing, and going across the world trying to woo Red China is another thing. Taking a controversial stand on NATO is certainly alarming, to say the least. But to ignore, to the extent it has, the massive problems of urban growth is not only an unacceptable policy but a ludicrous one, no matter what the minister may say while trying to blame this party and its leader for the government's own shortcomings.
Let me tell the House why this policy is ludicrous. The terms of reference of the task force on housing and urban development, which has since issued a report that requires urgent attention, were to examine housing and urban development in Canada and to 21545-38J
report on ways in which the federal government, in company with other levels of government and the private sector, could help meet the housing needs of all Canadians and contribute to the development of modern, vital cities. Thousands of dollars have been spent to give direction to the government, and recommendations have now been made. But the moment one mentions the problems of our cities to this government, it dons its cloak of inertia, which is also known as the constitutional straitjacket, and the Prime Minister expounds on the relationships of political theory to the constitution.
This convenient attitude of inertia is unwarranted and is neither understood nor accepted by millions of Canadians living in our cities who follow the Prime Minister and regard him as a modern Messiah or contemporary Pied Piper in the hope of being relieved of their frustrations caused by urban living. According to the task force report, our cities must come to grips with their major problems now. With pressures so great and problems so complex, tomorrow will not do. There is no point in the minister blaming the hon. member for Hamilton West for that.
I should like to refer to an editorial in the Hamilton Spectator for August 8, 1968, which stated that although local councils have been aware of their shortcomings for years, the cities do not have the resources or constitutional powers to solve them. The provinces and Ottawa have the authority to readjust priorities and initiate research and programs of aid, as well as to apply tax revenues where most needed. But only joint federal-provincial action can spare Canadian cities the horrors that afflict U.S. cities.
The editorial states the government must admit that the problems of urban development have become so acute that they have now become national problems and must be treated as such. One cannot deny that housing, urban transportation and pollution are national problems; but can we afford to sit back and be complacent in the light of the environmental malaise in our cities, such as economic poverty, social disorganization, mental and health breakdowns, anti-social acts, mental illness, alcoholism and drug usage? Are we to sit back and wait for the explosion which will give impetus to this Government to set up a commission to investigate the causes and prevention of violence? Are we to wait for this violent explosion before this Government moves? The quality

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
of life in the cities ranks as a national problem; as the cities go so goes the nation. To reject this proposition can only mean we are inviting disaster and chaos as a way of life in the cities.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
^Representatives of cities and towns, the provinces and Ottawa should be meeting to set the shape of city life for the future. The city representatives must be given an audience. They have the problems and perhaps they have the answers. They desire involvement. Let me read from the 32nd annual report of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. I refer to a statement made by Mayor Allan O'Brien, the newly elected president:
In my opinion, our first, priority is to get a firm commitment from the provinces as well as from the Federal Government to our right to be consulted on all the territory with which we are concerned that happens to be also of concern to the Federal Government. I think we should make sure we get that commitment to consultation before we take too firm stands for changes in the constitution, other than reference to the right of consultation.
That is all we are talking about here. We need a pipeline from the major cities to this Parliament in order that their representatives can reach the members who can then perhaps give some direction to this Government as a result of their deliberations.
The theme of urgency, as stated in the report of the task force, was adopted by the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras), a man I have learned to respect even though he will not give Hamilton any money. I hope in the very near future he will say to the hon. member for Hamilton West he now has the opportunity to reply to those requests. I hope he will say he has re-assessed his thinking on urban renewal and will honor those commitments which should have been honoured earlier by his predecessor. I hope he will tell me that we are going to get more money than we ever thought we might get. I am waiting for that statement. Let me just read what he said when he introduced Bill C-192 to amend the National Housing Act. These words were important then and they are equally important today. They appear at page 9174 of Hansard for May 28, 1969.
Another significant dimension is that Canada today is primarily an urban society. Almost three quarters of Canadians live in the larger towns, Cities and metropolitan areas. By 1980, it is estimated that more than 80 per cent of the population will be owning, renting, or hunting for shelter in

our urban centres. Current trends indicate that almost one third of these people will live in our three largest urban centres of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
The quality of life in these rapidly growing communities is a matter of serious concern. We have heard much and can expect to hear more about pollution, overcrowding, traffic congestion, inadequate recreational facilities, alienation, deprivation and the inertia of some of our institutions. These issues cannot be neglected indefinitely nor can they be resolved by the methods of the past.
Nor can they be solved quickly or easily, Mr. Speaker. No single level of Government, no one person, holds the key to their solution, or the formula for building better communities. The answers must be sought in joint planning and co-operative endeavours. We must seek ways for all levels of Government, together with interested citizens, to achieve an urban environment which offers the physical, social and cultural dimensions of healthy and creative living.
That is all we are trying to do, help the minister along with his theory. To me, this shows a desire for three level consultation. I think this idea has great merit. I want to know whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in answer to my question, will indicate that he is aware that the province of Ontario has invited advisers to this conference. I should like to hear a statement from the government that we can all depend upon the continued attendance of municipal representatives as a means of collecting views at this coming federal-provincial conference.
Let me quote from an editorial that appeared in the Hamilton Spectator on December 4, 1969 as follows:
It has become clear to just about everyone except influential members of the federal government that if Ottawa doesn't help the cities beat their traffic, slum, crime, poverty and other problems, the cities' plight will worsen.
So far, Prime Minister Trudeau's government has taken shelter behind a constitutional screen, pointing out that municipalities belong to the provinces, not to Ottawa.
As urban conditions unhappily demonstrate, neither the provinces nor the cities themselves have been able to correct the growing urban troubles. At best, the provinces and municipalities are maintaining services, not repairing the social and economic breakdowns, not coping successfully with the deficiency.
Steadfast in its myopia, Ottawa bluntly refuses to recognize urban deterioration as a national problem and rejects the proposal to establish municipal-federal dialogue.
There are others throughout this nation who feel as members on the backbenches feel. I do not have to mention names because they are printed everyday in the local newspapers. Let us not forget that in spite of the constitution there is ample evidence to suggest that
December 8, 1969

Ottawa has consistently had a strong and significant monopolistic role in urban affairs. Let us look at the record in respect of the physical presence of the federal government. One need only refer to airports and their services; housing through C.M.H.C.; all forms of rail, transportation and communication and the great many federal public building facilities, installations and Crown agencies. What has the federal government done in this regard? What about tariffs, freight rates, the taxation system, military bases, immigration, unemployment policies and labour mobility? What about the quality of life? If more evidence is required regarding federal leadership let us consider the complexities of urban growth, pollution, regulation of social behaviour, regulation of public and private health, social assistance, language and citizenship? It is, therefore, ridiculous and irresponsible to indicate that the federal government has no business in the cities and towns of this country. It is essential that this Government, after consultation with the provinces and municipalities, state what the policy is or what it is going to be with regard to urban affairs. I know there are a lot of members on the other side who want to hear such a statement, too. Something tells me they are in trouble when they go back home. I hope they will tell us what kind of trouble they are in.
Confusion among levels of government must be eliminated if the problems of our cities are to be solved. If confusion and conflict continue over what role who should play, if any, in solving the problems of urban growth the problems will get more acute and critical and the solutions will then be out of reach.
The task force report recognized the role the federal government should play, yet the recommendations have been ignored. My friend mentioned a few of them, and I shall just read a couple. At page 72, the report reads:
The federal government should establish a Department of Housing and Urban Affairs.
Then, at page 74, I read:
The federal government, through a new Department of Housing and Urban Affairs, encourage, support and co-ordinate an expanded urban research program with greater priority on the initiation of practical research programs, including pilot projects.
Page 75, of the report reads:
A new Department of Housing and Urban Affairs should give early priority to the creation of a central information bank to collect, organize and
Urban Problems
disseminate available data on these subjects to other governments, agencies, and Canadians generally.
An article in the Telegram of November 25, 1969 under the heading "Ottawa needs the
cities" reads in part:
Prime Minister Trudeau and his government must not hide behind a legalistic barrier in dealing with the growing problems and needs of Canadian cities.
Constitutional restrictions aside, most Canadians now live in the urban reaches of this country. Most of the advanced technology coming our way, the funds to pay for it, the human resources to manage it, will all come from the cities. We have not yet reached the incredible U.S. situation where 70 per cent of Americans live in one per cent of their land space. But we are heading very fast in that direction.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Further on it reads:
And most people in Canada now are in the cities.
They will demand higher priority for city needs. Participatory democracy may yet outweigh constitutional restrictions as the Prime Minister now emphasizes them.
In conclusion-and I say this in all sincerity because I know all hon. members are equally concerned about the problems which we face-let me say that the challenge of urban growth is one of tremendous significance. We must stop wasting time nit-picking like the minister; we must stop wasting money; we must stop alienating the urban dweller. We must begin to work in harmony and co-operation with all levels of government so that the enormous task with which we are confronted can be attacked systematically and expeditiously with a view to reaching practical solutions from which all will ultimately benefit.

As a representative of a constituency which includes a portion of metropolitan Toronto, but most of which borders on the northern limits of that area, I have a very special interest in the future development of our cities. These cities are growing at an unprecedented rate and this rate is accelerating. It is projected that the population growth in the Toronto region will in the next 20 years be greater than that of the past 150 years, from something in excess of 2J million people to at least 5 million, and up to 7 million people. One projection is that one out of every three Canadians will be living in the Montreal and Toronto regions before the end of the century. The other cities across our land will experience similar growth. Many towns will become cities, and villages will become towns.
With these certainties ahead of us, governments-and I use the plural advisedly-and politicians who fail to give serious attention to these matters are guilty of inexcusable irresponsibility. Equally irresponsible are those who continue to give lip service to the problem for which they are legitimately responsible, while trying to pass off the responsibility for its solutions to other levels of government.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I am getting sick and tired of attending meetings, seminars and think-ins and hearing the experts in the field enumerate the problems without providing any rational solutions. When they are told about the jurisdictional problems, they slough

them off with the comment that they are sick and tired of politicians who are fiddling over constitutional problems while the people burn. Actually, everyone is right to be sick and tired while we fail to come to grips with one of our major concerns. But being sick and tired is not good enough. It is not good enough because we happen to be a federal state, we happen to have a constitution, and we happen to have provinces which have rights and responsibilities under that constitution.
We also happen to have cities which are creatures of the provinces. Our people are taxpayers and voters who pay their taxes to all three levels of government, and many, but regrettably not most, who vote at all three levels. These people are also getting sick and tired. If they are not now, they will be when the price of our neglect manifests itself in greater pollution, greater congestion, even less adequate but more expensive housing, larger areas of blight and poverty, broken homes, increased delinquency, and the terrors which can beset big cities which have grown and the only planning has been by the short-range marketplace.
These people, the voters, have a right to criticize us as federal representatives, because about 70 per cent of them voted for or against us. They do not really have the right to criticize us for their own failure to turn out in similar numbers at provincial and municipal elections in order to ensure that they get the type of representative who will fulfil his responsibilities. I realize that this is not entirely fair becanse we do not always fulfil our responsibilities to the extent that we should or would wish, and displays of selfrighteousness will not be particularly constructive in reaching solutions. As a matter of fact, to really come to grips with the problems will require a degree of political statesmanship and maturity which we have rarely evidenced in the past.
Therefore, I would like to make some specific proposals. The first is a repetition of one that I have made on previous occasions in the House, most recently in the Throne Speech debate on October 27. This proposal is for a national institute of urban and transportation studies. I combine urban and transportation studies because the two are so intimately interlocked. We are fortunate in this country to have specialists in urban planning who rank with the best in the world, and their work could be far better co-ordinated by such an institute. Other countries are
December 8, 1969

somewhat ahead of us in the field of transportation, although the Canadian Transport Commission is attracting staff of particularly high calibre from other countries, and we welcome them. France is well ahead in the field of air-cushion vehicles, and Japan is well advanced in high-speed trains of the conventional and jet-propelled types.
It seems redundant for each province to duplicate research in these fields, and a cooperative effort could benefit all parts of Canada. Such an institute could well be associated with one of the major universities in the country, or perhaps it could be coordinated by a national secretariat with the research and studies in specific fields being allocated to each of several universities across the country. I favour the approach through the universities rather than as part of the government bureaucracy because there would be greater flexibility and fluidity than government tends to generate, as we have experienced. This approach would also have the advantage of turning out graduates who would become specialists to man the civil service which will run our urban centres or city states in the future. Such an institute could be of international stature and attract experts of world renown to its faculty or as visiting lecturers. I think this will more likely be accomplished by having a centralized institute at the graduate level.
My second proposal is one which calls for the political statesmanship and maturity which I mentioned previously. It is for a meeting of the private, elected representatives of all parties at all three levels of government to discuss the problems of our major urban areas and try to find ways to resolve them. If a reasonable measure of agreement is achieved we would then return to our respective legislatures, be they federal, provincial or municipal, and fight for the adoption of such agreed-upon procedures.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
If I may be excused for seeming parochial, I wish to use the Metropolitan Toronto Planning Area as an example, because it is the one with which I am most familiar. Attendance would be by all elected representatives, at all three levels, covering each of the municipalities in metro itself, plus those adjoining municipalities such as the townships of Markham, Vaughan, Mississauga and Pickering, and possibly Peel, York and Ontario counties. As this will involve possibly 150 to 200 or more men and women, each level would have to appoint spokesmen to act
Urban Problems
on their behalf at the sessions. This would require meetings beforehand to agree upon general positions and prepare position papers. Amendments beyond reasonable limits would have to be ratified by the caucus of each group. Hopefully, there would also be observers from other major urban centres across the country and interested independent groups such as the Board of Trade and the Bureau of Municipal Research.
The first area with which such a conference could deal is one in which there is an existing and legitimate federal presence such as airports, harbours, railways, post offices, Crown corporations, urban renewal projects and a myriad of other federal agencies. In METPAC, which is the Toronto federal Liberal caucus, we have divided ourselves up into areas of specialty. For example, the hon. member for York West specializes in waterfront development, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead) the Post Office, the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) airports, the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Deakon) railways and overpasses. Others have other specialties.

He is the chairman. With like specialization at the provincial and municipal levels, co-ordinated political dialogue and cooperation would be on a continuing basis. These specialists do not act completely on their own but take direction from and report back to their caucuses. With such a procedure we would have a tri-level pipeline into which we would all be plugged. At present we work in our own three little vacuums all too often, and wonder why people are surprised or upset. Frequently two of the vacuums get together and leave the third, usually the municipality, out in left field. That may not be scientifically correct, Mr. Speaker, but that seems to be the way it operates. Such a procedure is still not very easy to accomplish; there is no guarantee of success, but even a small step toward progress by politicians would be a giant step forward for the taxpayers.
The next stage of such a tri-level seminar would deal with our frustrating but very real constitutional considerations. As I understand our federal government's position, Mr. Speaker, we have no objection to moving further into urban areas if this is agreed to be desirable and if we are invited to do so by those

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
who have this right and responsibility. While I cannot speak for the government, it is my belief that we will not simply act as tax collectors and as passive benevolent bankers or sugar-daddies.
If agreement can be reached we would accept our responsibility for action, for policies and for financing, including the unpopular job of raising the necessary taxes. We would not, I suggest, nor should we, simply turn over money which is spent without our control. A recent sad experience in this regard relating to medicare should be ample evidence of how this system can backfire. It is incredible how much more careful one is with his own money than with that which is someone else's. It is like expense account living.
If the other jurisdictions do not want to give up their rights and responsibilities- those two words must always be used together-then they must have the courage to take the ultimate political responsibility of taxing to do the job, or the other side of that which is to take responsibility for not doing the job. In either case the electorate will judge, but that is one of the ways parties and politicians are re-elected or defeated, and that is what democracy is all about. You have to take the basic decision and be responsible to the taxpayers, or else do not act and be responsible for not acting.
I therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the second phase of the tri-level conference be devoted to finding areas wherein we can reach some measure of agreement on shifts of responsibility which require constitutional change. Again, we can return to our respective legislatures and put our agreed-upon position to our government, thus exerting legitimate pressures which represent the feelings of the elected representatives. Should this prove successful-and there is no guarantee that it will, of course-we could schedule subsequent conferences on a bi-monthly or quarterly basis to deal with specific projects that we decide upon. The first of these could well be the excellent proposal for a regional airport authority, suggested by my colleague from Etobicoke. This is a perfect example of the type of program that could be achieved by thoughful consultation and co-operation at all levels.
I am not suggesting this as an ideal answer, or as the only answer, but it is a suggestion and an experiment worth trying unless someone has something better to offer. I have discussed these general proposals with senior 
elected officials at all three levels of government and have received gratifying encouragement. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this type of mechanism might well provide the vehicle, together with the centre for urban and transportation studies, for coming to grips with the realities of the seventies. The British North American Act was drafted for the realities of another age.
It is up to those of us representing the burgeoning urban areas at all levels of government to stop talking out of three sides of our collective mouths and straining our credibility in the eyes of the taxpayer. We may live to see the bills come in for our failure to get together; but if we do not, our children will, and their judgment on our performance will probably not be flattering. That is, Mr. Speaker, if our children live, for a report of the United Nations, with the authority of the Secretary General, tells us that if we do not reverse the tide of environmental pollution within ten years the process will become irreversible and the earth will die; the land will not support crops, nor will the air and sea support life. Our days will be numbered.
The great irony is that we are spending all of our efforts in many directions. We are worrying about the city of the future when, in fact, there may not be any future to worry about. I suppose you do not believe this, Mr. Speaker. Neither do I. It is so immense and so horrible that our minds automatically reject it. I suppose it does not matter very much if it is the truth; or does it?

Mr. Speaker, we came here this afternoon to discuss a very simple motion asking the government to consider the advisability of this House setting up a committee to look into the problems of urban development. We in this party have gone even further; we have suggested that there be established a department of housing and urban development, with a full-time minister in charge of it.
The debate this afternoon, if it has done nothing else, has shown very clearly that so far as the government is concerned it is not yet prepared to grapple in any realistic way with the problems of urban development. That is something which has been evident for a good many years. Talk how he will, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) knows that for many years housing has been considered completely unworthy of having a portfolio to itself. Mr. Speaker, I am
December 8, 1969

Urban Problems
sorry to see the President of the Privy Council leaving the chamber, because if he does so I shall have to do my best to deal with him in his absence. Responsibility for housing has over the past few years been moved from pillar to post through half a dozen departments. Now we Anally have a Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) in charge of housing, but housing is not yet considered deserving of a full-time minister. All of this proves the government's unwillingness to deal with the problems of the cities.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This afternoon the President of the Privy Council rose and in effect told the House that he cares little about the matter under discussion, namely, how to deal with urban problems in Canada, because he did not even go near the subject during his 20-minute speech. He used the whole time as a diversionary tactic to talk about practically anything else. He stood there as a name-dropper introducing us to many interesting characters all around Canada, including some of the provincial premiers and other people, all of this to draw attention away from the government's complete bankruptcy of ideas and lack of interest when it comes to doing anything about urban affairs. It was this bankruptcy of ideas which not so long ago led to the resignation of the then minister who was supposed to be-again it was a part-time portfolio-in charge of housing matters.
The people of this country deserve something better, Mr. Speaker. Why in the world does this government get the reports of the Economic Council if they do not read them? The 1967 report of the Economic Council of Canada states that one of the most urgent priorities for the entire country at all levels of government is the growing problems of the urban districts, the great conurbations now being built which, by 1980, mean that at least one-third of the people in Canada will be crowded into three urban centres, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
All the problems of pollution, overcrowding, violence, lack of privacy, fresh air, space, tensions and disorder that we have heard about this afternoon will be aggravated by then, but the spokesmen of this government stand up and say cheerfully, "Other people have not wanted to do anything about this in the past, nor shall we. Let us leave it to some other level of government." What kind of statesmanship is that?

I do not want any more points of privilege during my speech unless I am given double time for each one. The problem of the cities being built today is that they are a mess. They do not correspond with the needs of the people who live in them. They have not been kept up-to-date and we find ourselves with horse-and-buggy cities in the jet age. When we speak about the need for slum clearance here, low rental housing there and areas for recreation yonder, we are trying our best to patch up the mess but we are not dealing with the problems of the cities as they should be dealt with. They are getting more out of date all the time and have against them the great indictment that they are defeating, disillusioning, devitalizing and dehumanizing the people who live in them.
It is many years since that great Scotsman, Patrick Geddes, pointed out that if we are not careful all our cities will become like New York on a larger scale, with people moved into those canyons of stone away from green things, growing things, light and sunshine, where they will lose their human character when deprived of those natural elements that make us human beings. We are allowing that process to go on and on and on.
Today we come into this House and say, "Now let's make a simple attempt to have the representatives of the people deal with recommendations the Economic Council has been making for years, saying that urban development is one of the major problems of our time." But we are given the brush-off by the President of the Privy Council doing a lot of knit-picking exercises instead of coming to grips with this problem. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, the great United States sociologist Lewis Mumford said a few years ago what I think our objectives should be as we examine today's problems in our cities. He said:
The final test of an economic system is not the tons of iron, the tanks of oil, or the miles of textiles that it produces; the final test lies in its ultimate products ... the sort of men and women it nurtures, and the order and beauty and sanity of their communities.

That was written a few years ago. In his book "1976: Agenda for Tomorrow," in 1968 Stewart Udall, United States Secretary of the Interior had this to say:
We plan and act on a vast scale when it comes to space and defence. But by some obscure alchemy our will is feeble when attention turns to the blighted urban areas where most of us live. It is tragic that at this very moment we are using only a small fraction of our technological prowess on problem-solving in the cities. But the future is promising because we have the resources to achieve an American renaissance. Through continuous sound management of the economy, our annual gross national product should rise above the two trillion level within two decades. Unless false objectives cause us to use our extra wealth on illusory arms races or dubious military actions, or on idle displays of conspicuous consumption, we can achieve goals heretofore beyond the horizons of our hopes. These we have. The question is, rather, one of a national will and the formation of a common commitment to great civilizing goals.
Stewart Udall has a true conception of the tremendous task facing us on this continent in rebuilding our big urban areas. He says that nothing short of a new commitment will suffice, because only then will we undertake the job of rebuilding our cities and recreating in our people at the same time the spirit of hope and enterprise. In one election campaign the Premier of British Columbia coined the slogan, "Men to match our mountains." If we free our mountains of smog and other forms of pollution we shall be able to build in Vancouver men and women to match the mountains.
If the committee we advocate is set up with the new department, we also advocate, it will mean that we shall be able to study the problems of the cities and make proposals for action, not in the dim and distant future but in our lifetime. Some of the problem areas that will have to be discussed, and there are many, involve urban and suburban sprawl, traffic and transportation, housing and recreation, pollution, alienation and poverty; and questions of fresh air, sunshine and green growing things which are fast disappearing from our cities. Our cities are slowly becoming not fit for human beings. That is especially true when green growing things disappear and the cities become canyons of stone.
Some of the other problems involve questions of finance and jurisdiction for cities, and last but by no means least, the necessity of participation by citizens in those matters involving them. These are the things such a committee will have to study. It should be, in
December 8, 1969

the first place, a committee that will undertake steady action and not be forever studying, researching, white papering and task forcing, if I may use those expressions, and so on. Instead, it should make recommendations as it goes along; they should be short-range recommendations made in the light of long range objectives. In the second place, it ought to study the question of the role the federal government should play in solving the problems of the cities. That role, I believe, is a double one involving the setting up of some kinds of federal standards or guidelines. Also, I believe that our cities are entitled to obtain a percentage of federal funds necessary for urban development and growth, because that is essential if they are to solve their problems.
Times are changing and the rigidities of the present constitution bother many people. I do not think that some of us are even beginning to visualize what constitutional changes may be necessary in the 1970s. In that connection may I read to the House submissions made by two active Vancouver aldermen. They say:
A practical solution to the problems of the cities in the 70s would be to allocate a share of the income tax directly to the cities. It would probably be desirable to make the allocation directly to the larger cities and indirectly, through the provinces, to the smaller cities. In this way, the cities could get on with the job of making cities more livable and keping property taxes at a reasonable level.
That solution does not sound too difficult to these men. Those in municipal administration know what must be done if we are to undertake the big job of rebuilding our cities that is so necessary. The furnishing of funds to municipalities will be one of the biggest problems involving urban development. May I add one thing, Mr. Speaker. We have done this sort of thing in Canada and we could do it again if we put our minds to it. At Expo we saw the greatest commitment that I have seen during my lifetime on the part of our people to join wholeheartedly in a Canada-wide venture. They did so because they knew that it involved them all, that it was their Expo and their concern. When we undertook to build Expo, all the federal government's resources and ingenuity were employed in the hope of making the venture a success. We saw nationwide planning. Each locality in turn was asked to plan its share of the activities and its share of involvement. Citizens were encouraged to give of their best, whether they were in ordinary jobs or were hon. members of this House. Firm deadlines had to be met and people of all races, cultures and origins
Urban Problems
co-operated to make possible this great venture.
Because of Expo we developed in this country a heightened sense of purpose and identity as Canadians. I remember a French speaking taxi driver telling me in Montreal not too long ago how proud he was of having played a part in Expo. He had not worried then about who his neighbour was, so long as he was working on the same project. He said to me, "I wish once again that we could feel as we felt when Expo was being developed." The millions of Canadians from coast to coast who went to Expo to see and enjoy the colourful sights and sounds wished, after the doors were closed, that it could all be revived. In my view we can revive something like that, but on a much larger scale. We can apply the same principles we applied to Expo if we can obtain the same commitment from our governments, beginning with the federal government, for the big job of rebuilding our cities.
This, Mr. Speaker, is what must be our goal for the 1970s. Our major goal must be the rebuilding of Canada's cities from coast to coast. If Ottawa takes the lead and assumes its proper responsibilities toward the other levels of government in making certain that there is a fair allocation of resources, I think we can do an outstanding job of rebuilding Canada's cities and increasing at the same time our stature as Canadians.

speechtext: I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative Party has in the past had very little to say about the cities. It seems it has suddenly discovered the cities. To gain political advantage, the Official Opposition is in a desperate way now putting a motion before us which I hope to show in a very few minutes is transparent. It is transparent because it is shadow-boxing and fancy footwork. I do not think that shadow-boxing and fancy footwork will persuade the government or the Canadian people that they understand the situation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The thought that occurs to me is this: if you have no ideas, what is the best ploy to use? It is to suggest the formation of another committee in the hope that someone else may come up with an idea. Poverty, housing, transportation, health and welfare, immigration, citizenship and manpower retraining are all matters which affect the lives of people living in the urban centres. All these things can now be discussed by our standing committees; all of them have been discussed and can be discussed again by them. What we do not need is yet another committee.
I think that new mechanisms are desirable to bring federal, provincial and municipal authorities into some sort of direct relationship. The problems of the cities are local and specific; we cannot pronounce upon them at the national level. The task of implementing solutions for them will not be accomplished by yet another committee; it will be accomplished at the local level by those within the urban community who are most involved. This is the lesson we have learned in the course of more than a hundred years. How much say will the cities have in determining the kind of cities they will become?
We need to ask ourselves such questions as these: How large are the cities to become? What kind of cities will they be? What kind of urban environment should be preferred? What recreational areas, transportation facilities, housing and services should they enjoy? These are not questions which will be decided by any committee of this House for each of the separate communities of Canada. These decisions will be made by the communities themselves.
The representatives of the cities will have to make themselves heard. They must speak out. Too often their voices have been muted by provincial governments which have conned them into feeling they are obliged to accept only what those provincial governments make available to them. Many municipal representatives have been inhibited, when it comes to speaking out, because they could see no hope. Part of the usefulness of this debate might lie in saying to these representatives of the cities that we are concerned about their difficulties and are prepared to

support their efforts. But they will have to make more noise and present their case forcefully to provincial governments. Though it is all very well to talk about new mechanisms, we must come down in the end to specific cases. In this connection there is one such situation which would lend itself readily to a new mechanism. I refer to the planning of a metropolitan Toronto airport system to serve the metropolitan region not necessarily, for example, a region confined by the borders of the existing metropolitan community but one which would include five airports which are already functioning.
I spoke on this subject during an earlier debate and I shall not go into it in great detail now. A new approach to airport planning is needed. We need a planning board composed of officials, one in which all four levels of government are engaged-the federal government through the Department of Transport, the provincial government through as many as four different provincial departments, regional government and, lastly, the boroughs concerned. It should also include those most directly involved, the senior elected representatives of the boroughs who are accountable to the people. In a very special way they understand the aspirations of the people who have elected them. Such a board as I am suggesting would advise the Department of Transport and the departments of the provincial governments affected. Its function should be planning. It is necessary to put the municipalities back into the planning process at the very beginning. The hon. member for North York (Mr. Danson) referred to this in his speech. The old "ladder system", by which the federal government discusses projects or responsibilities with the provincial government which, in turn, discusses them with the municipalities, is no longer working. Too often the apparatus at the provincial level acts as a filter, passing along only what it wants to pass along. Indeed, I suspect the filter process works both ways. In place of the ladder I believe we should substitute the round table; the representatives of the municipalities should sit around this table with the other authorities concerned, at the very beginning of the planning process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this Parliament we have heard much talk of urban
December 8, 1969



renewal, the provision of public housing, lower interest rates and so-called guidelines, all of which we hope will have a beneficial effect on the serious problems of housing and urban renewal which are facing Canada.
We are all familiar with the Task Force on Housing which was headed by the former Minister of Transport who was responsible for housing, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). I am sure we are all aware of the report which he presented to this House, I believe in January or February of this year. We are familiar, too, with the recommendations of the report and the stand that was taken by the former minister. It was the complete indifference shown by his colleagues in cabinet to the problems of housing and urban renewal that forced the minister to resign. The minister was completely repudiated by his colleagues, and this being the case I am sure we give him full credit for resigning.
I am sure all members agree that discussion and study do not of themselves build new homes or initiate badly needed urban renewal schemes. It is obvious that Canadians have heard enough words and are now ready for the ring of hammers building homes, for the carrying through of urban renewal schemes which all of us know are badly needed in Canada. I think it is obvious, too, to most Canadians that even before the task force left Ottawa the members of the task force knew, as we did, pretty well 100 per cent the problems facing Canada and 90 per cent of the solutions to those problems.
The recommendation dealing with the removal of the sales tax on building materials used in residential construction, which I might add met with the unanimous approval and support of all Canadians, was ignored by this government. The argument used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson)-I presume he was speaking for his colleagues in cabinet-was that the $300 million collected each year by this tax would have to be made up elsewhere. I am sure all reasonable members of the House would agree that this amount would have to be made up. We fully agree that if the 11 per cent sales tax were abolished, the $300 million collected would in all probability have to be raised from some other source. I think I can also say that we were unanimous in our contention that if this were the case and the money had to be collected from elsewhere, we should find a source less crucial to the national well-being of the Canadian public than the field of housing.
Urban Problems
I think it is obvious to all Canadians and to the members of this House that this government has been playing around with the serious problems of housing and urban renewal that are facing the average wage earner of Canada at the present time. Through CMHC the government has been turning funds on and off like water coming out of a tap, much to the dismay of those Canadian citizens on the bottom half of the income ladder, especially those who are forced to live and raise their families in the slums and ghettoes of our cities and for whom the promise of a just society has little meaning. I think it has become obvious to the average Canadian, certainly to those of us on this side of the House, that the present government has become bankrupt of ideas in matters relating to the solution of housing and urban renewal problems, which we feel is the No. 1 domestic problem in Canada at the present time.
Apart from the serious housing problem facing Canada, we have other requirements, such as the implementation of a transportation system that will overcome choked streets, clogged highways and overcrowded airports. Our air and our water must be cleaned up. Housing and its related problems are a total challenge. In the matter of urban renewal I have a very special interest, because for almost a decade now, certainly for more than five years, a large number of families in that section of my riding known as the Mundy Pond development area have become political pawns of this government. They have been fed a continuous diet of promises, of grandiose plans and schemes which to this date are as far from realization as when they were conceived almost 10 years ago.
In this same development area-I am sure this is true in many other parts of Canada- properties have been frozen; permits to effect necessary repairs have been refused; people have not been allowed to build necessary extensions to their properties to accommodate their larger families; repairs and improvements, other than those which are necessary to keep the homes wind and watertight in accordance with city by-laws and government regulations, are forbidden because the government has promised to implement so-called urban renewal schemes.
In a great many cases in my riding, people are forced to live under conditions that are almost indescribable, conditions under which no human being should be forced to live. While these people are suffering, the government sticks its head in the sand, adopting the

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
old ostrich psychology of pretending that all is well; that if it keeps its head in the sand long enough, the problems will disappear; that through the wave of a magic wand the problems facing these people in the have-not areas of Canada and in our cities will vanish.
While I have a great deal of sympathy for people in the underprivileged countries of the world, I sometimes feel that in Canada perhaps we need additional aid to improve conditions in our ghettoes and slums. I sometimes think that although we have a great deal of sympathy for people of other countries who are suffering untold agony as a result of their economic conditions, there are areas in my riding where assistance is badly needed in order to give people the chance to live like decent, respectable Canadians, a status to which I think they are entitled.
I am not one to ignore what has been done. In my own riding, and indeed in many major cities in Canada, a lot has been done to provide reasonably good public housing for our underprivileged and average income citizens. I feel that much more must be done in order to give the people at the bottom half of our income ladder a chance to live in dignity and raise their families under conditions to which they are entitled in this twentieth century. I could cite a number of cases in my own riding where people are living under conditions that are completely and utterly indescribable.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In this 20th century we have put men on the moon and satellites in space, yet the people to whom I refer do not enjoy the benefits of indoor toilet facilities. It is a terrible indie ment of this government that people in this day and age should be forced to live under those conditions. I do not think we can take pride in the fact that we have skyscrapers in certain parts of the country and an affluent society, while in other parts of the country people are forced to live under conditions not in keeping with the 20th century.
The former Minister of Transport responsible for housing travelled the length and breadth of Canada at considerable expense to the Canadian taxpayer. He received briefs from various people and associations. He came back and presented a report which all of us thought was reasonable. This man, the hon. member for Trinity, made a report in which he recommended certain things. The bulk of those recommendations was not accepted. He recommended the abolition of

the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. This was not accepted. These recommendations were for the most part rejected by the former minister's cabinet colleagues, and we know what happened. The minister, being an honourable man with pride, could not stand the thought of being repudiated by his colleagues. Consequently he resigned and is now sitting as a private member of this House.
We must assume that the former minister made recommendations in his task force report based on information gathered from all parts of Canada and from all segments of our population. He listened to groups and individuals. We felt that by and large his recommendations were sound and reflected the feeling of the average Canadian taxpayer. If this government was seriously interested in solving these problems, it would have taken the necessary action to implement most of the recommendations, especially the one dealing with the 11 per cent sales tax. Instead of accepting the recommendations of the task force appointed by it, the government elected to ignore them. In doing so it ignored the sentiments and feelings of the average wage earner across Canada.
The former minister resigned and the present minister was appointed to fill the gap. In accepting the responsibilities formerly held by the hon. member for Trinity in his role of being responsible for housing, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) was being dishonest. I feel he was being dishonest because he accepted a role which he knew was completely unpopular and not in keeping with the feelings and wishes of the Canadian public. The former minister made recommendations that were not acceptable, yet the present minister was prepared to step in and act as the minister responsible for housing. In doing so I contend he is being dishonest to himself and to the Canadian taxpayer.

The matter of housing is very serious and important to Canadians. Urban renewal is very important. In my riding the people have been promised an urban renewal scheme for almost ten years. This has left the people living in hope, while being prohibited from making necessary repairs and building extensions to their property. They have been waiting for this grandiose urban renewal scheme. This is grossly unfair, and the minister and the government should be ashamed of themselves for allowing these people to believe that Utopia is just around the corner.
The government should give serious thought to implementing the urban renewal schemes it has promised. The government and the minister know that the Mundy Pond urban renewal scheme has been promised for five, six or seven years. The people in that area do not deserve the treatment they have been accorded by this government by continuously promising a grandiose scheme which has never materialized. I have grave doubts that it will materialize in the next five years.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I think that in many respects the government did tell lies, because I can remember that two or three years ago people were led to believe that this scheme would take place within so many months. The people concerned were elated about the prospect of
being given water and sewer systems, half decent housing, streets and sidewalks; but after almost a decade they are still left up in the air. I feel that the time has come when this government must stop pussyfooting. It must begin to show a little compassion for the Canadian people and make good some of the promises it made to the Canadian people and specifically to the people in my riding. Those promises after almost ten years continue to be symbolic of all those made by the present government-that	is, broken promises.
Tonight I call on the minister responsible for housing to give great thought to this serious problem because he is dealing with human lives.
