subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
I welcome this debate, Mr. Speaker, and I congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for starting it. I am impressed on most counts by the deep concern about cities expressed by hon. members, and I believe it accurately reflects many general concerns that have been expressed by people living in most of our urban areas.
In my relatively brief tenure as minister responsible for housing I have become very much aware of Canada's serious urban problem. Within the time available to me I have walked some of the streets and talked with people in many urban renewal areas and public housing projects. I will repeat what I said generally in my statement on second reading, that poverty, pollution, frustration, alienation and social unrest do have unique urban dimensions and may reach serious levels in our major metropolitan areas if we neglect the problems.
I must say, however, in all honesty that some of the debate has been superficial. There is an incredible gap between observing a concern, registering a generalization of concern, and in identifying precisely our problem and then beginning to deal with it in terms of effective policy-making. The gap is immense. It is immense because the first, essential requirement for bridging that gap is to understand, and what we do not yet have in the House at this level of government-or, I suggest, at any other level of government-is a precise and meaningful understanding of our urban environment and its problems.
I have become increasingly conscious, as I have talked with people, both housing experts

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
and people directly affected, that the urban system is an incredibly complicated one. Any view we take of it these days is rather like a snapshot that is out of date the minute it is taken, because it is a snapshot of the working out of the urbanization process that has become the central feature of this country's socio-economic development. Because it is the central feature, all the complex forces of development have come to focus on our cities; the effect of migration and rural adjustment, industrialization, technological progress, and many more forces that are at work in this country. To complicate matters, particularly in determining corrective policies, one must recognize that if these broad forces have played a major role in shaping our urbanization process, each city has been responding and adapting to them in a unique way peculiar to itself, so that each city is developing its own peculiar characteristics and problems and will require its own specific responses.
Out of all these processes have emerged urban units in this country-this has taken place everywhere else in this world-that are highly complex, socio-economic systems. I think the thing that has impressed itself on me more than anything else is that each part of the social system that is a city and an urban area is highly interdependent in ways that defy simple analysis. I am stressing these points because I sincerely believe that many of us are failing to appreciate how little we understand about this system. The reaction to this problem is to urge us as a federal government to act now without understanding but with serious consequences for the cities and for those most in need of our help.
Let me merely outline, in answer to some of the comments made earlier this evening and this afternoon, some of the most recent of such policies of our government and of other governments, by way of illustration. Let me outline some of the immediate, ad hoc and fragmented responses. Urban renewal was launched with the best intentions to help relieve the serious housing difficulties of the urban poor of this country. But in the process we understood far too little of the complex working of the housing markets, social groups and urban economy. As a result, in the name of urban renewal we occasionally helped destroy viable communities and inflicted hardship on precisely those we were seeking to assist. Public housing, stemming also from similar good intentions, has on occasions led to the locking of the poor into even more rigid social ghettoes.

Those are two examples of where the federal government has been guilty, in which we have participated and in which we have to effect corrections. But there are others-and I am not pointing the finger at any level of government. One has to look at what is going on in many of our major urban areas, in terms of expressways. The downtown cores of the cities are congested. There is a demand for building expressways to join the suburbs to the downtown city core. This will mean more cars, which will in turn need wider expressways, which will in turn require more parking lots. As a result, the land in the core of the cities increases in cost and the urban poor who so often live in these areas are denied access to decent housing because of the high cost of land. Assessments go up in the downtown area, and so do the taxes. Businesses in the downtown area see this trend and head off to the suburbs where they can get cheaper land and production, and so the whole cycle reverses itself all over again. These are some of the ad hoc responses of which governments in nearly all highly populated and industrialized nations have been guilty.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
To go back to urban renewal, Mr. Speaker, hon. members are aware of the fact that in August of this year, following discussions with the responsible ministers from all the provinces, I affirmed my predecessor's decision regarding the urban renewal program, and since that time I have carefully reviewed the whole nature of that program. We have had extensive exchanges with the provinces on this subject on the basis of our analysis and findings, and upon completion of the discussions this week with provincial ministers who are in Ottawa I shall make a detailed statement in the House explaining our actions.
As hon. members also know, a similar review of public housing is currently under way. I hope we will be able to announce shortly our policy with respect to this matter, with reference particularly to the 1970 program, but I give fair warning now that it is essential that we receive all the provincial recommendations, have an opportunity to digest them, and then go back to the provincial ministers to get some kind of consensus before the recommendations are locked in.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
I appreciate the question, Mr. Speaker. Yes, I have been consulting representatives of the municipalities too, I think with the consent and support of the provincial ministers, by my meetings with the representatives of the Executive Committee of the Association of Mayors and Municipalities, who recently sent me their views on both urban renewal and public housing guidelines, for which I thank them, and which are now being digested.
While I am on the subject of this question, Mr. Speaker, may I respond to a comment made earlier in this debate by an hon. member opposite who implied that the invitation of the Premier of Ontario to municipal representatives to attend this week's federal-provincial conference was in the face of resistance by the federal government. This is not a fair statement of the case. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 22 and again on June 3 clearly indicated that municipal representatives at federal-provincial conferences would be welcome, but made the straightforward and legitimate proviso that since the municipalities report constitutionally to the provincial governments, if the municipal representatives came in it would have to be at the initiative of the provincial governments. I uphold and applaud the presence in Ottawa today of municipal representatives from Ontario but, Mr. Speaker, let us call a spade a spade and allow this contradiction to the comment previously made. I repeat that there was no opposition from the federal government to their presence at this conference.
I have referred to the need for a careful review of existing programs of urban renewal and of all the housing programs under the National Housing Act. That analysis of the existing programs marks the first phase of our attempt to understand this complicated urban process. I say also that the second phase necessarily involves an incredibly deep and careful analysis of that process in all its complexity. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I have launched an intensive inquiry into the workings of the whole urban area, the whole urban process in our country. I expect and hope to be able to place recommendations before my colleagues in the late spring.
Urban Problems
I make no apologies for suggesting that this matter requires further study. I have talked with many people in this country and to many people from other countries, so-called urban experts, certainly people who were concerned about urban problems in their own country, and I find somewhat to my horror that I know of no country, not even among the most advanced industrial western nations, that truly has an urban policy. It is a complex, complicated process. It will require deep analysis, and no superficiality is going to give us answers that are significant. In fact, any failure to dig deeply into this process could do more harm than good.
We are primarily trying to learn how best to deal with the critical urban problems. For example, we want to know who are the urban poor. Are they in the main unemployable, or are they temporarily unemployed? No evidence collected to date permits us to answer even this simple question. We want to know why there is such a squeeze on the revenues of urban governments, and what can be done about it. We want to know what alternatives there are to the current treadmill of more cars, more highways, and then more cars. We want to know what alternatives there are to monotonous suburbs and decaying inner cities.
But part of the problem, and I plead with hon. members to understand this, or join me in the attempt to understand it, in trying to answer these specific questions is that they cannot be answered or dealt with in isolation. Where you put a public housing project of any significant size, where you put an airport or an expressway, has a shaping effect on urban society. These matters are interrelated, and they cannot be dealt with as has been the case in the past, as if the city was a multiring circus and what was going on in one ring had no relationship to what was going on in the other rings.

speechtext: That is why you have to be in there.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
We will be in there, Mr. Speaker; that I can assure the Leader of the Opposition, and I hope he will join me in the process because this is beyond partisan debate so far as I am concerned. Superficial response and political opportunism will not help us to deal with this problem. We have to understand fully how the problems arise. We have to start treating them not in terms of their symptoms but in terms of their causes. We

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
also need better data on how they are connected to social, demographic and economic Change.
To do so we are now trying to analyse the process of urbanization in Canada, and now being well into it I realize the colossal undertaking it is. Once we are able to isolate the key determinants, we will be able to isolate and evaluate the possible alternative strategies for governmental intervention to manage that system effectively. Its objective is to direct the urban system so as to alleviate the critical urban problems and to pursue actively our primary social goals in a country which is becoming essentially urban. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not so presumptuous, and I would challenge anybody to be so presumptuous, as to believe that we will be able to solve all our Urban problems as a result. However, I can assure hon. members we will be moving toward greater knowledge about them, not on a superficial, fragmented, ad hoc basis, and we will better understand the role we as a federal government might play therein.
Central to this approach is a keen awareness of the responsibilities of the provinces and their municipalities in the whole area of the urban process. To ensure that their interests and their legitimate roles are kept continually to the forefront I shall launch discussions with the responsible ministers of the provinces. It is my hope we will work very closely together to arrive at a joint consensus of goals and strategies. I was heartened to learn that the Leader of the Opposition has called for a conference on urban policy within his own party. I trust this means that he agrees with us that understanding is the prerequisite of effective action. Forming committees, decrying inaction and proposing ineffective policies, these are the tactics of those who seek to trivialize and make political capital from our urban problems, not solve them.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I regret to be critical, but this afternoon in the House and in recent discussions I have heard some of this superficial approach to the problems of our city. Surely it is easy to talk of increasing the need to co-ordinate existing federal activities in the cities, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition and as I have been guilty of doing. But we must co-ordinate these activities-and I have added this reservation-in terms of the objectives and the conception of the urban process.
Surely, to do an effective job we must address ourselves to advancing and getting 
answers to these questions. Would hon. members suggest, Mr. Speaker, that I expand the federal urban renewal program, as the hon. member from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and one of his colleagues suggests, and then seek-and only God knows how-to co-ordinate such a confused action with other federal activities in the cities? This, Mr. Speaker, is what several hon. members from across the floor have suggested. My answer is no, we should not do this.
We are all fully aware of the seriousness of the problems. The fact that the vast majority of members of this House, and most particularly of this government, represent urban ridings has ensured that recognition on our part. What we seek are solutions, not sops; effectiveness, not emotion; and relevance, not rhetoric. We are playing our part. We have been-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before getting into the text of my remarks on the debate on this very vital question of transportation, I wonder if I might direct a word or two to our distinguished President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and some of his colleagues on the treasury benches. I should like to remind them that once in a while it is good to listen to what one's neighbours are saying. Just before dinner the President of the Privy Council chastized those of us on this side of the House for not supporting a proposition which invites federal participation and, indeed, active federal leadership in solving urgent problems. He stated that the federal government must not involve itself in matters essentially within the purview and the responsibility of municipalities. But in a reply to a question by my leader, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) stated that he was indeed involved in discussions with municipalities.
December 8, 1969

In the last few years, Mr. Speaker, it has sometimes appeared to Canadians from all walks of life that the right hand of government has not the vaguest idea what the left hand is doing. In the course of his remarks the President of the Privy Council led us in this chamber to believe that levels of government other than federal were responsible for holding up programs in such places as Don Vale and Trefann Court. I should like to remind the President of the Privy Council of the remarks made by the Minister without Portfolio to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) very recently. At page 1589 of Hansard of December 4, when the hon. member for Hamilton West asked whether the apparent deadline of December 31, 1969, affecting such programs as Don Vale would come and go without any communication from the federal government on action to be taken before the end of the year, the minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, when I met with residents representing the Don Vale urban renewal committee I made it quite clear that it was most unlikely we would be able to.have legislation available because it would require the setting up of rehabilitation grants and loans inherent in their proposal. I made it quite clear to them, regretfully, that that was the situation and that this was unlikely to take place before December 31, 1969.
May I just tell the minister that his remarks in the debate this afternoon, apart from being grossly inaccurate in many respects were far removed from his plea about the urgency of removing the whole question of urban problems from the sordid arena of partisan politics. If the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) is interested in the capacity of the municipalities to deal with their own problems, I should like to cite one or two facts to him.
I should like to read from the report of the Technical Advisory Committee on Urban Transportation of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. Table XII entitled "Average Yearly Capital Expenditures on Roads" is based on study recommendations and scales of expenditure required to meet programs deemed necessary by these municipalities. Then, immediately after, comes the amount of money each urban centre involved is required to pour into the program. For Vancouver the figure is $12 million, based on a $60 million, five-year program. But over those five years all they have to spend is $3 million, or approximately 25 per cent. Ottawa-Hull, $24,871,000; projected scale of budget expenditures, $9,933,000; Hamilton, $12 million; projected scale of
Urban Problems
budget expenditures, $9,200,000; London, Ontario, $3 million; projected, $690,000; Victoria, $3 million; projected, $649,000. Perhaps those figures will give the hon. member for Etobicoke some idea of the magnitude of the problems we are talking about.
Mr. Speaker, in all discussions in this House about the great urban problems in Canada today, not one member has spoken in any meaningful way about the most costly aspect of urban renewal, that is urban transportation, mass transit problems, the problems of intra-urban communication and the difficulty of removing alienation brought about by the inability to communicate with one another in terms of transportation.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
In September, 1964, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities started what will go down in history as the first major study of urban transportation in Canada. The ensuing studies and work conducted by what most hon. members know to be a very active committee culminated about a year ago in the first urban transportation conference ever held in Canadian history. What took place at the conference is a matter of record although, I am afraid, it is fast passing into history.
My participation in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is to highlight our existing concerns in problems of urban transportation both in this country and in the United States. I believe the minister was incorrect when he said that no western country has an urban philosophy and is doing nothing about the subject except trying to understand it. Perhaps in that process of understanding they have not evolved an "a, b, c" governing urban philosophy and underlying principles; but by God, they have not stood still and done nothing about the problem. They are doing something about it. I think it is fair to say that no federal government of this country has become involved in any significant manner in the field of urban transportation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext: That is true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The government's entry into the trans-Canada highway program might be held by some to be an exception to this point. I contend that those who conceived the trans-Canada highway program did not intentionally try to resolve the urban transportation problems of any particular area. In some areas like Montreal the highway does play a part in solving problems; it links the

December 8, 1969
Urban Problems
three main cities in the central core with the south shore of the St. Lawrence, but this is only incidental. The highway was not intended to solve any major problems in areas of urban transportation. There are other minor exceptions to the rule which I will cite in a moment, because enumerating the exceptions I think will strengthen the main point of my argument.
Through the National Capital Commission the federal government has poured millions of dollars into a system of parkways in Ottawa. There is also the recently announced parkway to be built out to the Ottawa Airport. If the government had not announced the construction of this road I would have been tempted in my remarks this evening to direct a question to the minister responsible for railways, canals and telegraphs and ask him to remove the fallen branches and trees from the cow path leading to this city's international airport.
In addition to the two examples I have cited, there are minor ones such as the involvement of the National Harbours Board in the construction of bridges across the St. Lawrence at Montreal and, I think, across the harbour at Vancouver. One or two other small projects could be mentioned. But my being able to identify those areas of federal government involvement in matters of urban transportation shows that that involvement is so limited, so much a "one shot" affair as not to count at all.
In its urban renewal program the government accepts no responsibility whatever for matters pertaining to urban transport and the impact those federal renewal programs, as well as other programs, will have on the ability of the cities to solve their transportation problems. Yet is it not strange that in writing about the human problems of the city our greatest modern writers refer continually to the theme of alienation? Inevitably, when one talks to our young people, one finds that they are alienated from society in no small measure because they cannot communicate with their friends through the use of transportation facilities.
May I touch on one other area of the federal government's involvement in transportation matters. I refer to the development of above-grade crossings over railway lines crossing our principal highways. I mention this matter now because I hope that increased costs involving the construction of these raised crossings designed to eliminate present day level-crossings will not reach the
[Mr. Forrestall.l
point where the federal government will feel it incumbent to curtail them and suggest to responsible departments that the program of building such above-grade crossings be cut back. We must have above-grade crossings if our highways are to remain safe and if highspeed users of our highways, such as they are, are to continue to find it safe to drive over them.
I emphasize again that the federal government's involvement in four or five separate areas does not mean that it has become involved in matters of transportation. It is easy to argue that way. Rather, such scant involvement makes it abundantly plain that the government has no plan to become involved; that talk on the matter has not even begun; that action has not begun and that, as is painfully obvious, the government has no intention of helping with the development of urban transportation. It does not wish to become involved in parallel developments involving broad urban transportation philosophy, notwithstanding, I submit, what the minister hopes will be done next spring.
May I contrast our record with that of the United States. To do so may I read from the report of the Technical Advisory Committee to the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. I quote from page 23 of the report as follows:
By contrast the federal government in the United States is playing a steadily increasing role, both with respect to urban highways and urban mass transit.
Unlike this country's programs, federal aid in the United States began with aid to rural highway programs. From 1944 on, however, we have been able to discern that the United States government's direct involvement in the construction of major arterial systems has been growing. This tendency which was started about 26 years ago has now expanded to the point where in 1965 $3,675 million had been poured into that general field. The United States federal assistance to the mass transit sector of its economy is of more recent origin, but its history can be traced back to 1960 when with the support of the presidential nominee John F. Kennedy, the Democratic Party placed urban affairs as a national issue in their party platform and pledged:
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Federal aid for comprehensive metropolitan transportation programs, including bus and rail transit. Commuter railroads as well as urban highway programs and construction of civil airports.
December 8, 1969

At that time Kennedy declared:
That the Democratic Party in the United States knows of no wiser investment that this nation could make than federal aid to urban transportation.
Those were wise words ten years ago, Mr. Speaker, and I think they are fitting today. I commend them to the minister in the formulation of any policy he is preparing for presentation to his colleagues. The direct result of that position by President Kennedy was the passage in that country of the housing act of 1961 which, while modest in its start, at least provided $50 million in federal loans for acquisition and improvement for mass transportation facilities in urban areas of the United States. An additional $25 million or $30 million was also allocated at that time, and I commend this to the minister. It was committed for urban transportation projects, mass transit projects. The minister has no terms of reference to do that. I hope in his thinking this winter he comes up with some terms of reference and will include it.

Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) calls for the establishment of a committee of the House to deal with urban problems. The amendment moved on behalf of our party by my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) called for the establishment of a department of housing and urban affairs. We must realize that 75 per cent of the people of Canada now live in our cities. They are faced with tremendous problems such as urban transportation, housing, pollution and education. These problems must be solved. It is surprising that the government does not agree that the establishment of a committee and a department are worth-while objectives which it ought to support. I suggest the reason for that is very simple. The government is caught in the constitutional trap of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The cities are the creatures of the provinces and therefore the federal government cannot deal with urban problems.
It is for that reason we heard the foolish speech of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), which I will refer to later, and the speech of the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras). I
Urban Problems
have a great deal of respect for the Minister without Portfolio. He is going to study the problem. If he is as successful in delineating the problems of housing as he was in delineating the problems of the Indians, he will be fired from this job in the same way he was fired from his last job. The minister told the House, "Let us not do anything now, because what the opposition are proposing are ad hoc, fragmentary policies." I cannot think of a better way to get rid of ad hoc, fragmentary policies than to have a House committee and a department of urban affairs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE TO ESTABLISH COMMITTEE ON URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
I listened with amazement to the foolish speech made this afternoon by the President of the Privy Council blaming the Leader of the Opposition for this motion. Why? Because the Leader of the Opposition last year agreed to a motion setting up the standing committees of the House. As we all know, the motion on which we voted was the one the government would agree to, and nothing else.
The minister is not foolish, but why did he make such a foolish speech? It is because he wanted to draw the attention of the House and the public away from the legitimate criticisms being made, not just on this side of the House but by his own members. We remember that the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) resigned from the Liberal Party because of the inaction of the government with regard to urban affairs. We know about the very excellent speeches that are made outside this house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens). The Globe and Mail for November 25 reported his activities at the recent policy conference of the Liberal Party at Harrison Hot Springs in the following terms:
Member of Parliament Philip Givens crystallized the opposition when he got the mike and demanded to know if this conference was going to urge a federal initiative to help the cities. He got cheers. In the corridor later he also got the raspberry from the Prime Minister, who contended that the constitution gave the cities to the provinces, which could raise their own taxes if they wanted to aid the cities.
I think the hon. member for York West is right. I wonder why he has not made that speech here. This is where Members of Parliament are supposed to make their main speeches. Why did he go outside this chamber to make this speech, if he really means what he says. I could not pass up an opportunity to speak in this debate without referring to the

December 8. 1969
Urban Problems
former minister of transport, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), who resigned his portfolio because of his disagreement with the government and the Prime Minister. It is not important that hon. members do not agree with every proposal of the Task Force on Housing headed by the former minister of transport. Some of the recommendations were good and with some I disagree. For example, I disagree with the former minister and the present minister that it has been made government policy not to go ahead with urban renewal plans because there are some things wrong with public housing as it now exists. Of course there is a great deal wrong with public housing projects, but I submit to the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing that with all their faults they are still far superior to the kind of housing which the people who now live in these projects had prior to moving into them; they are far superior to the slums from whence these people came. It is a disgrace for the minister to stop plans for more public housing. He should not permit it.
I want to put on record one or two comments made by the hon. member for Trinity when he resigned as minister of transport and minister in charge of housing. I quote from an article in the April 25 edition of the Toronto Telegram:
It is really part of a larger issue-the constitutional concept of federalism-and perhaps the Prime Minister's concept that housing and urban affairs are not really a federal responsibility-
"We are talking about a theory of federalism which is not what many people think it is. It is a theory of 10 almost autonomous provinces held together by a fairly weak federal government."
The Prime Minister answers every call, whether it be from this or the other side, from members like the hon. member for York West who has been conspicuous by his silence on this subject in the House. The former minister of transport answered every demand for action in solving the problems of urban living by hiding behind the constitution. We do not believe that is an excuse, Mr. Speaker. We believe the constitution were made for people, not people for the constitution.
We believe there are amendments through which the constitution could be used for the federal government to take the initiative in meeting with the cities to go into details of the difficulties and how they can be dealt with.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The hon. member for Etobicoke suggested that the municipalities were not aware of the

nature of these difficulties. I wonder where he has been for the past 20 years. Does he not know that the municipalities, through their organization of mayors and municipalities, has for years been making representations to the federal government asking for help in slum clearance, urban renewal, public housing, urban transportation, pollution control, provision of sewers and water systems. Help in all these fields has been requested for the last 20 years by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. But every year the answer has come from the government, and particularly from the present Prime Minister that the government cannot do these things because they are provincial responsibilities; the cities have to direct their requests to the provincial governments.
We think it is time for a new deal, one in which the 75 per cent of the people who live in our cities would be consulted through their governments. We think the way to consult them is by establishing a department of urban and housing affairs. We feel the government can and should do this. We hope the Prime Minister will learn a lesson from the demands which are being made, and will begin to act.
